cards.t: How common hypertension is, and how few people have it controlled
q: how common is hypertension
how many people with hypertension are controlled
does hypertension rise with age
cards.x:
Hypertension is common and poorly controlled. Counting a reading of 130/80 or higher or being on medication, 47.7% of adults have it. Prevalence climbs steeply with age: 23.4% at ages 18 to 39, 52.5% at 40 to 59, and 71.6% at 60 and over. It is common in middle and older age but not restricted to it.

The control numbers are the real story. Only 59.2% of those affected are aware they have it, 51.2% are treated, and just 20.7% are controlled. Each step drops off, so many people who are treated are still not at goal.

cards.t: Primary (essential) hypertension: what it is and who gets it
q: what is primary hypertension
what causes essential hypertension
what are the risk factors for hypertension
cards.x:
Primary (essential) hypertension is persistently high blood pressure with no single identifiable cause. It makes up about 90 to 95% of all hypertension. Instead of one cause, it comes from inherited susceptibility (many genes, each contributing a little) interacting with environmental exposures over time, so it is a combination of mechanisms.

The risk factors are advancing age, family history, excess (especially central) body fat, high dietary sodium, physical inactivity, excess alcohol, dyslipidemia (abnormal blood fats) and insulin resistance.

Quick way to tell it from secondary hypertension: in secondary hypertension one identifiable underlying condition or exposure is driving the pressure. In primary hypertension there is no such single cause.

cards.t: Why blood pressure stays high in primary hypertension
q: why does blood pressure go up in essential hypertension
how does angiotensin II raise blood pressure
what is impaired natriuresis
cards.x:
Several mechanisms push pressure up together, and none alone explains primary hypertension.
- Vascular narrowing raises resistance, so the heart pushes against more opposition.
- Sympathetic nervous system activation raises heart rate and cardiac output.
- The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) adds to it: angiotensin II tightens the blood vessels and triggers release of aldosterone, which makes the body hold on to salt and water.
- Impaired natriuresis means the kidneys need a higher pressure before they will excrete salt, so pressure settles at a higher level.

cards.t: Hypertensive emergency: what defines it and how it is recognized
q: what is a hypertensive emergency
what blood pressure defines a hypertensive emergency
what organ injuries occur in a hypertensive emergency
cards.x:
A hypertensive emergency is severely high blood pressure together with acute organ injury caused by that pressure. The organ injury, not the number, defines it. There is no absolute cutoff: it is often above 180 systolic and/or above 120 diastolic, but lower values qualify when there is injury, and severe pressure without acute organ injury is not an emergency.

Examples of qualifying injuries are hypertensive encephalopathy (brain dysfunction from the pressure), acute pulmonary edema, acute kidney injury, aortic dissection and acute coronary syndrome. Red flags are confusion, seizures, altered consciousness, visual disturbance, focal deficit, abrupt severe headache, chest or back pain, shortness of breath and oliguria (very little urine), and swelling of the optic disc on fundoscopy.

Do not delay while awaiting repeat visits. The workup looks for the injured organ: electrocardiogram, troponin, B-type natriuretic peptide, kidney tests, urgent brain imaging for neurologic signs, and a chest radiograph for pulmonary edema or a widened mediastinum.

cards.t: Treating a hypertensive emergency
q: how is a hypertensive emergency treated
what drug is used for pulmonary edema in a hypertensive emergency
why use an intravenous drug in a hypertensive emergency
cards.x:
A hypertensive emergency is treated like any emergency first: stabilize the airway, breathing and circulation, get intravenous access, and monitor continuously. Then use a titratable intravenous drug, meaning one whose effect can be turned up or down quickly, matched to whichever organ syndrome is present.

The pressure comes down in a controlled way, not all at once: the mean arterial pressure falls by no more than 20 to 25% in the first hour, to about 160/100 to 110 over 2 to 6 hours, and to normal over 24 to 48 hours. Aortic dissection and some strokes are the exceptions. Lowering it too fast risks stroke, myocardial injury and kidney failure.

When the injury is pulmonary edema, the treatment is intravenous nitroglycerin or nitroprusside, oxygen or positive airway pressure support, and a loop diuretic if the patient is overloaded with fluid.

cards.t: Hypertensive urgency (an outdated term) and severe asymptomatic hypertension
q: what is hypertensive urgency
is 226/128 a hypertensive emergency
what is the difference between hypertensive urgency and emergency
cards.x:
Hypertensive urgency is a term that is no longer used. It referred to severe blood pressure elevation, typically systolic 180 or higher and/or diastolic 110 to 120 or higher, without signs of acute, life-threatening organ damage.

The key point is what separates it from an emergency: organ injury. The same number in an asymptomatic outpatient, such as 226/128, is not an emergency because there is no acute organ injury. The pressure alone never makes it one.

cards.t: Resistant hypertension and the look-alikes to exclude first
q: what is resistant hypertension
what causes apparent resistant hypertension
what should you check before calling hypertension resistant
cards.x:
Resistant hypertension means blood pressure stays above goal despite three antihypertensives from different, complementary classes at the maximally tolerated doses. Before using that label, rule out the look-alikes (apparent resistance): medication nonadherence is the most common cause, along with measurement error (cuff size, technique), white coat effect, high sodium or alcohol intake, interfering drugs such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and stimulants, and undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnea or secondary hypertension.

So confirm adherence, cuff size and technique first, use out-of-office readings to exclude white coat effect, and screen for secondary causes (an aldosterone-renin ratio after correcting low potassium, and a sleep study). True resistance is itself a clue to a secondary cause, for example when there is low potassium, or snoring with witnessed apneas.

cards.t: Secondary hypertension: causes and when to look for one
q: what is secondary hypertension
when should you suspect secondary hypertension
what are the common causes of secondary hypertension
cards.x:
Secondary hypertension is high blood pressure caused by an identifiable underlying condition or exposure. Estimates are about 5 to 25% of hypertension, varying with the population and how hard it is sought. The common causes are obstructive sleep apnea, chronic kidney disease, primary aldosteronism, drugs and alcohol, and renovascular disease. Uncommon ones are underactive or overactive thyroid, pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, aortic coarctation, and Cushing syndrome.

Go looking when the course departs from gradual primary hypertension: early onset, abrupt new onset, resistant pressure, or sudden loss of prior control. Other clues are unexplained low potassium, organ damage out of proportion to the pressure, abnormal kidney function, snoring and apneas, attacks of headache and sweating, and proximal weakness.

Testing follows the suspected cause: an aldosterone-renin ratio, plasma or urine metanephrines, cortisol testing, kidney artery imaging, a sleep study, or thyroid-stimulating hormone.

cards.t: Hypertension caused by chronic kidney disease
q: how does chronic kidney disease cause hypertension
why is hypertension and kidney disease a vicious cycle
how do you treat hypertension in chronic kidney disease
cards.x:
Hypertension from chronic kidney disease runs both ways: kidney disease raises blood pressure, and uncontrolled pressure speeds up kidney injury. Chronic kidney disease means a kidney abnormality lasting at least 3 months (typical causes are diabetic nephropathy, glomerular disease and polycystic kidney disease), and hypertension is present in over 80% of patients with chronic renal failure.

Why pressure rises: the kidneys excrete sodium poorly, so fluid outside the cells expands; the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and sympathetic activation raise vascular resistance; and the hypertension raises pressure inside the glomeruli (the kidney's filters), scarring them. That is the vicious cycle.

Look for raised creatinine or reduced filtration rate, albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio shows damage before filtration rate falls), blood or casts in the urine, edema, and structural disease on imaging. Treatment is to control pressure and sodium retention, using an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker when albuminuria is present, which also protects the kidney.

cards.t: Renovascular hypertension from renal artery stenosis
q: what is renal artery stenosis
what is fibromuscular dysplasia
when should renal artery stenosis be suspected
how do you test for renal artery stenosis
cards.x:
Renovascular hypertension is high blood pressure caused by narrowing of a kidney artery (renal artery stenosis). There are two types. Atherosclerotic stenosis occurs in older patients with established vascular disease and is often bilateral, with progressive kidney decline. Fibromuscular dysplasia affects younger women: a non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic disease of the vessel wall, with abnormal cell growth causing narrowing and bulges, a 'string-of-beads' look.

Suspect it with resistant or abrupt blood pressure elevation, an abdominal bruit (a whooshing sound heard over the artery), asymmetric kidneys, recurrent flash pulmonary edema, or a marked rise in creatinine after starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker. Renal artery duplex ultrasound is the first-line screen; the catheter renal angiogram is the gold standard, reserved for selected cases and for planning intervention.

Many atherosclerotic lesions are managed with medicine. Revascularization helps most with flash pulmonary edema, progressive renal decline or refractory pressure, so refer early. Do not use ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers in severe bilateral stenosis or stenosis of a solitary kidney.

cards.t: Primary aldosteronism: causes, screening and treatment
q: what is primary aldosteronism
who should be screened for primary aldosteronism
how is primary aldosteronism diagnosed
why does primary aldosteronism cause low potassium
cards.x:
Primary aldosteronism means the adrenal glands make aldosterone on their own, independent of the renin-angiotensin system. The sources are aldosterone-producing adenomas or bilateral idiopathic hyperaldosteronism. Excess aldosterone makes the body retain sodium and lose potassium, with metabolic alkalosis. The result is hypertension, often with no obvious electrolyte abnormality; if potassium is low it can cause weakness, cramps, polyuria and nocturia.

Screen when blood pressure is resistant, with unexplained or diuretic-induced low potassium, an adrenal incidentaloma (an adrenal mass found by chance), early-onset or familial hypertension (or early stroke), or obstructive sleep apnea.

The screening test is a morning seated plasma aldosterone to plasma renin activity ratio, positive if above 20:1 to 30:1 with aldosterone above 15 to 20 ng/dL. Correct low potassium first, since it falsely lowers the ratio. Endocrinology confirms with a saline suppression test, and adrenal computed tomography (CT) with contrast looks for an adenoma. Unilateral adrenalectomy is definitive for an adenoma, and spironolactone or eplerenone are valuable.

cards.t: Obstructive sleep apnea and hypertension
q: how does sleep apnea cause hypertension
what is blunted nocturnal dipping
does CPAP fix hypertension from sleep apnea
cards.x:
Obstructive sleep apnea is a secondary cause of hypertension, and the most common one listed. The airway repeatedly closes during sleep, causing intermittent hypoxemia (drops in oxygen) and brief arousals. That produces sustained sympathetic activation, which causes vasoconstriction and fluid retention, and blunts nocturnal dipping, meaning blood pressure fails to fall normally during sleep. Obesity is the risk factor named.

Clues are loud snoring, witnessed apneas, gasping, nonrestorative sleep, daytime sleepiness, obesity, and resistant or nocturnal hypertension. A short screening questionnaire asks about snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, blood pressure, body mass index, age, neck circumference and gender; a score of 5 or more is high risk. Confirm with polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing.

Treat the apnea with continuous positive airway pressure and keep giving blood pressure treatment, because that machine alone does not reliably normalize pressure. Blunted dipping is closely linked to cardiovascular risk.

cards.t: Drug-induced and alcohol-related hypertension
q: which drugs cause hypertension
why do NSAIDs raise blood pressure
can stopping clonidine or alcohol raise blood pressure
cards.x:
Many medicines, substances and supplements can cause or worsen hypertension, so a thorough review of everything the patient takes is the key step. That includes over-the-counter drugs, recreational substances and adherence. The list includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and corticosteroids; stimulants, decongestants (pseudoephedrine), cocaine and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors; estrogen contraceptives, calcineurin inhibitors, erythropoietin and some cancer therapies; excess alcohol or alcohol withdrawal; licorice and herbal supplements; and stopping clonidine abruptly.

Why: NSAIDs and corticosteroids cause sodium and water retention and blunt the effect of blood pressure drugs. Sympathomimetics (drugs that act like the sympathetic nervous system) raise adrenergic tone and vascular resistance. Alcohol withdrawal or abrupt clonidine withdrawal can produce acute severe (rebound) hypertension.

cards.t: Thyroid disease and hypertension: overactive versus underactive
q: how does hyperthyroidism affect blood pressure
how does hypothyroidism affect blood pressure
what is the first test for thyroid-related hypertension
cards.x:
Both an overactive and an underactive thyroid can cause secondary hypertension, through different routes. It is an uncommon cause, under 1% each.
- Hyperthyroidism increases cardiac output, so it mainly raises systolic pressure. Look for tachycardia, warm moist skin, heat intolerance, tremulousness, palpitations, weight loss, eye signs and goiter (an enlarged thyroid).
- Hypothyroidism increases vascular resistance, so it often raises the diastolic pressure. Look for bradycardia, dry skin, cold intolerance, constipation, hoarseness and weight gain.

The first-line screen is thyroid-stimulating hormone, followed by thyroid hormone levels as indicated. It is also a baseline test in all hypertension.

cards.t: Cushing syndrome as a cause of hypertension
q: how does Cushing syndrome cause hypertension
what are the signs of Cushing syndrome
how is Cushing syndrome tested
cards.x:
Cushing syndrome is a state of glucocorticoid (steroid hormone) excess, and it is a rare cause of secondary hypertension (under 0.1% in the table of causes). The excess glucocorticoid promotes sodium retention and vasopressor sensitivity, meaning the vessels respond more strongly to blood-pressure-raising signals.

Clues are proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, thin skin, broad purple striae (stretch marks wider than 1 cm), central adiposity and a rounded face, along with rapid central weight gain, facial plethora (a red, flushed face), depression and hyperglycemia. When the picture fits, test with a 24-hour urinary cortisol, a late-night salivary cortisol, or a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test.

cards.t: Pheochromocytoma: the catecholamine tumor that causes attacks of hypertension
q: what is pheochromocytoma
what are the 5 Ps of pheochromocytoma
how do you test for pheochromocytoma
cards.x:
Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor, usually in the adrenal medulla, that secretes catecholamines (adrenaline-like stress hormones). The excess causes sustained or paroxysmal (attack-like) hypertension. Episodes, sometimes continuous, bring the five Ps: pressure (headache), perspiration, palpitations, pallor and tremor. The paroxysmal triad is severe headache, sweating and palpitations.

A quirk: catecholamine vasoconstriction causes volume contraction, so the patient can also have orthostatic hypotension and orthostatic symptoms, hypertensive and orthostatic at once.

Think of it with a family history of pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1, or an adrenal incidentaloma. Test with plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines, which are highly sensitive.

cards.t: Why alpha blockade comes before beta blockade in pheochromocytoma
q: why give an alpha blocker before a beta blocker in pheochromocytoma
what happens if you give a beta blocker alone in pheochromocytoma
cards.x:
In pheochromocytoma, treat with alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine) before beta blockade (propranolol). The tumor's catecholamines cause vasoconstriction through alpha receptors. If a beta blocker is given alone, that alpha-mediated vasoconstriction is left unopposed, and the result can be a hypertensive crisis. So the alpha blocker has to be in place first, and the order is not negotiable.

The patient is also referred to endocrinology.

cards.t: Coarctation of the aorta and its blood pressure clues
q: what is coarctation of the aorta
how do you recognize coarctation on exam
how is coarctation diagnosed and treated
cards.x:
Coarctation of the aorta is a narrowing of the aorta, and it should come to mind in a young adult (under 30) with hypertension. The telltale pattern is high pressure in the arms with weak or delayed femoral pulses (radial-femoral delay). Comparing arm and leg pressures confirms the suspicion: normally the leg systolic pressure is higher than the arm's, so a leg pressure that is lower is the telling finding.

You may also hear a whooshing, 'machine-like' systolic murmur at the back (left paravertebral interscapular area), or see a left thoracotomy scar if it was repaired.

An echocardiogram establishes the diagnosis, confirmed with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging. Refer to a vascular surgeon or structural cardiologist; treatment is transcatheter intervention (balloon angioplasty versus stent) or surgical repair.

cards.t: Hypertensive heart disease and left ventricular hypertrophy
k: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
q: what does hypertension do to the heart
what is left ventricular hypertrophy
does a normal electrocardiogram rule out hypertensive heart disease
cards.x:
Hypertensive heart disease is damage to the heart from chronic pressure overload. The left ventricle becomes thickened and stiff (left ventricular hypertrophy), and it relaxes poorly in diastole. Reduced compliance can lead to heart failure with preserved or reduced ejection fraction as the muscle decompensates, and impaired coronary reserve plus accelerated atherosclerosis can cause ischemia. Hypertrophy increases cardiovascular risk independently of the measured pressure.

Findings can include an extra heart sound (S4 gallop) or a sustained left ventricular impulse, heart failure, ischemia, and atrial and ventricular arrhythmias including atrial fibrillation. On the electrocardiogram, voltage criteria for hypertrophy are specific but not sensitive, and lateral ST depression with T-wave inversion is the strain pattern. A normal electrocardiogram or ejection fraction does not exclude disease. Effective blood pressure control can regress the hypertrophy and reduce heart failure risk.

cards.t: Hypertension and the brain: stroke, small-vessel disease and cognitive decline
q: how does hypertension cause stroke
what is chronic small-vessel injury
how does hypertension affect cognition
cards.x:
Hypertension injures the brain in two ways. It causes stroke, both ischemic stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage (bleeding into the brain). It also causes chronic small-vessel injury: a sustained systolic burden, even with a controlled diastolic pressure, damages the small vessels and produces white matter changes and lacunar infarcts (small strokes). The result can be progressive cognitive impairment even without a clinically evident stroke.

Evaluation is a thorough neurologic exam, with urgent computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging for acute deficits, severe headache or encephalopathy. Long-term blood pressure reduction is among the most effective ways to prevent stroke, so control early. Acute stroke follows a distinct blood pressure protocol. After a prior stroke or transient ischemic attack, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker and/or a thiazide is used.

cards.t: Hypertensive kidney disease (nephrosclerosis)
q: what is hypertensive nephrosclerosis
what are the earliest markers of hypertensive kidney damage
how does hypertension damage the kidney
cards.x:
Hypertensive kidney disease (nephrosclerosis) is kidney damage from chronic high pressure. It injures the renal vessels (nephrosclerosis), the glomeruli (glomerulosclerosis, scarring of the filters) and the interstitium (tubulointerstitial fibrosis, scarring of the tissue around the tubules).

The damage feeds itself: kidney injury amplifies hypertension through impaired sodium excretion and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, so the cycle accelerates if untreated.

Rising albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) and declining estimated filtration rate are the earliest markers, followed as trends over time. Check creatinine and a urinalysis for casts or blood, and rule out other causes such as diabetes, glomerulonephritis and obstruction. An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker is used in chronic kidney disease with albuminuria, because it protects the kidney.

cards.t: Aortic dissection: recognizing and imaging it
q: what is aortic dissection
what are the symptoms of aortic dissection
does a normal chest radiograph rule out aortic dissection
cards.x:
Aortic dissection is an intimal tear (a tear in the inner lining) with dissection of the aortic wall. It is an acute hypertension-mediated organ injury, because chronic hypertension increases the stress on the aortic wall.

It presents with abrupt, severe chest, back or abdominal pain, described as tearing or ripping and maximal at onset. Signs can include pulse deficits, asymmetric arm pressures, an aortic regurgitation murmur, or a new neurologic deficit. Having no pulse deficit does not exclude it.

Get immediate computed tomography angiography. A chest radiograph may show a widened mediastinum, but a normal film does not exclude dissection. It needs urgent cardiothoracic and vascular surgery involvement, and it is excluded from the general emergency pressure-lowering targets.

cards.t: Hypertension and accelerated atherosclerosis
q: how does hypertension cause atherosclerosis
what vascular diseases does hypertension cause
why treat total cardiovascular risk and not just blood pressure
cards.x:
High blood pressure speeds up atherosclerosis, the buildup of plaque in artery walls. The raised pressure causes endothelial shear stress (friction on the vessel lining), intimal injury, oxidation of low-density lipoprotein and smooth muscle proliferation, all of which accelerate plaque formation. Smoking, dyslipidemia, diabetes and inactivity amplify the risk synergistically.

The complications are coronary artery disease and acute myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack, and peripheral arterial disease (reduced distal pulses). Examine the pulses and vasculature, with targeted imaging for peripheral problems.

So treat total cardiovascular risk, not blood pressure alone: antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapy where indicated, and for coronary disease or angina, a beta blocker, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, and a calcium channel blocker.

cards.t: Hypertensive retinopathy: stages and what they mean
q: what are the stages of hypertensive retinopathy
what does AV nicking mean
why do fundoscopy in a new hypertension patient
cards.x:
Hypertensive retinopathy is progressive change in the retina's tiny blood vessels, and it is the most common hypertension-related eye disease. Fundoscopy is done in every newly diagnosed patient because it is the only noninvasive view of the vasculature; follow with an annual eye exam or retinal scans and referral to ophthalmology or optometry.
- Stage 1: generalized narrowing of the arterioles.
- Stage 2: focal narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, and copper wiring (an opacified arteriolar wall).
- Stage 3: flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots and hard exudates.
- Stage 4: optic disc swelling, a sign of acute hypertensive injury.

Generalized narrowing and nicking reflect current and previous pressure; focal narrowing, hemorrhages and exudates reflect current pressure only. Control can lead to regression. Retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk independent of pressure, and retinal arterial narrowing predicts future hypertension.

cards.t: White coat hypertension
q: what is white coat hypertension
how do you rule out white coat hypertension
why does white coat hypertension matter in resistant hypertension
cards.x:
White coat hypertension means blood pressure is elevated in the office but normal at home. Because the office reading may not reflect the person's true pressure, the way to sort it out is out-of-office monitoring, either at home or with an ambulatory monitor worn through the day.

It matters in one more place: white coat effect has to be excluded before anyone is labeled as having resistant hypertension. Even when it is the answer, it still requires surveillance rather than being forgotten.

Quick way to tell it from masked hypertension: white coat is high in the office and normal outside; masked is the reverse.

cards.t: Masked hypertension and masked uncontrolled hypertension
k: normal office high home blood pressure
q: what is masked hypertension
what is masked uncontrolled hypertension
why does masked hypertension matter
cards.x:
Masked hypertension is the opposite of white coat: blood pressure looks normal in the office but is elevated at home. Masked uncontrolled hypertension is the same trap in someone already on treatment, who seems controlled in the office but is not controlled at home.

Because the clinic number is reassuring, it is easy to miss, so confirming with out-of-office readings is essential in high-risk patients. It matters because it carries significant cardiovascular risk despite normal office readings.

cards.t: Building a differential diagnosis for hypotension (the VINDICATES memory aid)
q: what is VINDICATES
how do you build a differential diagnosis
how should a differential be broadened if all diagnoses share one cause
cards.x:
Building a differential means asking three things: what the problem is, what it could be confused with, and what is deadly and can't be missed. If all your diagnoses share one etiology, add at least one from two other sources, such as infection, an obstructive cause or a structural cause.

A memory aid for the categories is VINDICATES: vascular, infectious, neoplastic, degenerative or drugs, idiopathic or iatrogenic, congenital, autoimmune, trauma, and endocrine or metabolic. Run through them so a cause outside your first idea is not missed.

cards.t: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (autonomic failure)
q: what is neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
why does autonomic dysfunction cause low blood pressure on standing
what is the treatment for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
cards.x:
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a sustained drop in blood pressure on standing or sitting upright, caused by damage or dysfunction in the autonomic nervous system. It is seen in people with diabetes, a genetic disorder or an autoimmune disorder, and diabetes, Parkinson disease and multiple system atrophy are the examples.

The mechanism: the sympathetic nerve endings release too little norepinephrine, so the vessels do not constrict enough and the heart rate rises less than expected. The pattern is an orthostatic pressure drop with minimal heart rate increase, volume depletion usually absent, and autonomic symptoms often present.

Treatment is slow positional changes and treating the underlying cause. Midodrine is best for neurogenic syncope, but avoid it with supine hypertension, severe heart disease or chronic kidney disease. Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is usually an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone. Like midodrine, it can cause or worsen supine hypertension, so it needs the same caution.

cards.t: Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (volume loss and drugs)
q: what is non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
what causes non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
how is non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension treated
cards.x:
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a sustained drop in blood pressure on standing or sitting upright that is not caused by autonomic dysfunction. The causes are hypovolemia (low blood volume), medications and advanced age, with examples such as diarrhea, hemorrhage and diuretics, plus dehydration, blood loss and poor intake.

The mechanism is reduced cardiac output and/or impaired vasoconstriction without a primary autonomic disorder, so the brain is poorly perfused. Because the autonomic system works, the heart rate rises significantly, volume depletion is often present, and autonomic symptoms are usually absent. In one case, 138/78 with heart rate 68 lying down became 108/64 with heart rate 92 on standing, showing an intact baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic response.

Treatment is slow positional changes and treating the underlying cause, the real diagnosis. When the cause is a drug, reduce or remove the medication.

cards.t: Familial defective apolipoprotein B-100
q: what is familial defective apolipoprotein B-100
how common is familial defective apoB-100
how does it present
cards.x:
Familial defective apolipoprotein B-100 is an inherited cause of hypercholesterolemia, meaning raised low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol. The defect is in apolipoprotein B-100, the liver-made structural protein of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL), LDL and lipoprotein(a). It affects about 1 in 1500 people worldwide.

On examination there may be tendon xanthomas (nodules on tendons), and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease can occur. On the labs, it is LDL that is raised.

cards.t: Blood pressure categories, the 130/80 threshold and the treatment goal
q: what are the blood pressure categories
what blood pressure counts as stage 1 vs stage 2 hypertension
when do you start medication for stage 1 hypertension
what is the blood pressure goal
cards.x:
Adults fall into four blood pressure categories, judged on properly obtained average readings rather than one borderline reading:
- Normal: top number under 120 and bottom number under 80. Reassess in 1 year.
- Elevated: top number 120 to 129 and bottom number under 80. Lifestyle intervention.
- Stage 1: top number 130 to 139, or bottom number 80 to 89. A risk-based decision.
- Stage 2: top number 140 or higher, or bottom number 90 or higher. Lifestyle plus medication.
If the systolic (top) and diastolic (bottom) numbers fall into different categories, use the higher one: 128/78 is elevated, and 138/92 is stage 2.

For stage 1, medication is started in adults with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk of 7.5% or more, using the PREVENT equation to estimate that risk. The goal is the same number as the diagnostic threshold: treat to below 130/80, with values closer to 120/80 encouraged where appropriate.

cards.t: Why creatinine rises after starting an ACE inhibitor
k: bilateral renal artery stenosis ACE inhibitor
q: why does creatinine rise after an ACE inhibitor
what does a marked creatinine rise after an ACE inhibitor suggest
is the creatinine rise drug toxicity
cards.x:
A marked rise in creatinine after starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis. It points to the anatomy, not to drug toxicity.

The reason: in narrowed kidney arteries, filtration is being maintained by constriction of the efferent arteriole, the small vessel leaving the glomerulus. Blocking the renin-angiotensin system removes that constriction, so filtration falls and creatinine climbs. A hemodynamically significant stenosis (one that really restricts blood flow) in a solitary functioning kidney can do the same, because nothing else compensates.

cards.t: Target organ damage in hypertension: the six organs and their signatures
q: what organs does hypertension damage
what is target organ damage
what are the complications of hypertension
cards.x:
Hypertension damages six targets, and each has a signature.
- Heart: left ventricular hypertrophy (thickened muscle) with impaired relaxation, which independently raises risk and may progress to heart failure with preserved or reduced ejection fraction. A normal ejection fraction therefore does not reassure.
- Brain: both ischemic stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage, plus chronic small-vessel injury giving white matter change, lacunar infarcts and cognitive decline.
- Kidney: injury to vessels, glomeruli and interstitium. The earliest markers are a rising urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and a falling estimated filtration rate, watched as trends.
- Aorta: dissection.
- Arteries: accelerated atherosclerosis.
- Retina: a direct view of the small blood vessels.

cards.t: Hypertension symptoms: why it is silent, and urgent warning signs
q: does high blood pressure cause symptoms
why treat hypertension if the patient feels fine
which symptoms of hypertension need immediate evaluation
cards.x:
Most patients with mild to moderate primary hypertension have no reliable symptoms from it. Headache is common but nonspecific, so it cannot be used as a guide to the pressure. That is the reason to treat it anyway: it causes cumulative damage over years to the heart, brain, kidneys, aorta, arteries and retina, and most patients have no symptoms to warn them.

A few symptoms are different and need immediate evaluation, because each points to an organ under acute injury: confusion or seizures, visual disturbance or a focal deficit (a problem with one specific function), abrupt severe headache, chest or severe back pain, and oliguria (very little urine).

cards.t: How to measure blood pressure correctly
k: measuring blood pressure in both arms
why take blood pressure in both arms
q: how should blood pressure be measured
why measure blood pressure in both arms
what makes a blood pressure reading falsely high
cards.x:
A diagnosis rests on readings taken to standard, because poor technique inflates the number. Rest quietly for at least five minutes, empty the bladder, and avoid smoking, caffeine or vigorous activity for thirty minutes. Sit with your back supported, feet flat, legs uncrossed, and the bare arm supported at heart level, without talking. Use a cuff size matched to the arm circumference, take at least two readings, and document any departure from standard technique.

Not resting, talking, a sleeved arm and crossed legs each raise the reading. Measure both arms at the first visit to find any difference, and use the higher consistent arm afterward; an asymmetric reading also raises concern for acute aortic disease.

This matters because measurement error is one of the first things to exclude before calling a patient resistant: bad technique mimics true resistance exactly.

cards.t: Home blood pressure monitoring: how to do it and how to use it
q: how should home blood pressure be measured
why average home blood pressure readings
how many days of home blood pressure readings are needed
cards.x:
Home monitoring uses a validated upper-arm device. Take two readings a minute apart, in the morning and the evening, for seven days, and report the average. That schedule gives 28 readings (two at each of 14 sessions) to average.

The average is what matters, not any one reading. Overreacting to a single high outlier creates anxiety and leads to unnecessary changes in treatment, so patients are taught not to overreact to their highest single reading.

cards.t: Baseline tests for a new diagnosis of hypertension
k: when to get echocardiogram in hypertension
q: what tests do you order for newly diagnosed hypertension
when is a chest radiograph or echocardiogram needed in hypertension
why is a baseline panel done before starting drugs
cards.x:
Every new diagnosis gets a baseline set: creatinine with filtration rate, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, electrolytes, glucose or glycated hemoglobin, lipids, thyroid-stimulating hormone, a full blood count and urinalysis. These screen for secondary causes, measure organ damage, and set a baseline before drugs that move potassium and creatinine are started. Every new diagnosis also gets an electrocardiogram and fundoscopy (looking at the back of the eye).

On the electrocardiogram, voltage criteria for thickened heart muscle are specific but not sensitive, so a normal tracing does not exclude hypertensive heart disease.

Two tests are not routine. A chest radiograph is for shortness of breath or findings suggesting fluid in the lungs (pulmonary edema), a suspected enlarged heart (cardiomegaly), or a worry about a widened mediastinum (the space between the lungs). Echocardiography, an ultrasound of the heart, is for suspected heart failure, a significant murmur, thickening shown on the electrocardiogram, or unexplained shortness of breath.

cards.t: Lifestyle treatment for hypertension
q: what lifestyle changes lower blood pressure
what is the DASH diet
do lifestyle changes continue once medication starts
cards.x:
Lifestyle treatment is recommended at every blood pressure category, and it continues alongside drugs rather than being replaced by them. So even an elevated reading that does not yet need medication still gets lifestyle treatment.
- A Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) style eating pattern: fruit, vegetables, low-fat dairy and whole grains, with reduced sodium.
- About 150 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity, plus resistance training.
- Weight reduction: a sustained loss of 5 to 10 kilograms can meaningfully lower systolic pressure.
- Alcohol limited to low-risk amounts, and do not start alcohol for cardiovascular benefit.

These map onto the modifiable risk factors: excess weight, high sodium, inactivity and alcohol, with low potassium intake and poor sleep also on the list.

cards.t: First-line blood pressure drugs and how to start and build therapy
q: what are the first-line drugs for hypertension
how many drugs do you start in stage 1 vs stage 2
are beta blockers first-line for hypertension
cards.x:
For uncomplicated hypertension, three drug classes are first-line: thiazide-type diuretics (chlorthalidone preferred), renin-angiotensin blockers (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers) and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine. Beta blockers are not first-line; they are preferred only when another condition selects them, such as heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, a recent heart attack or ischemic heart disease.

How many to start: one first-line agent is reasonable in stage 1, and in stage 2 two complementary agents are considered, ideally in a single pill, because adherence is itself a main determinant of control. The preferred pairings are a renin-angiotensin blocker with either a dihydropyridine or a thiazide-type diuretic. If pressure is still above goal, build to the foundational three, all at maximally tolerated doses: a renin-angiotensin blocker, a dihydropyridine and a thiazide-type diuretic.

cards.t: Thiazide-type diuretics for hypertension: choice and monitoring
q: what should you monitor on a thiazide diuretic
which thiazide is preferred for hypertension
what are thiazide side effects
cards.x:
Chlorthalidone is the preferred thiazide-type diuretic. The standing monitoring for the class is electrolytes, uric acid and volume status, because of its characteristic problems:
- Hyponatremia (low sodium) and hypokalemia (low potassium).
- Hyperuricemia (high uric acid), which may precipitate gout.
- Volume depletion, which matters especially in older adults.

Risk of low sodium is greatest where sodium is already low-normal. At age 65 and over, check sodium, particularly in women and in those with low-normal sodium. Combining a thiazide with a beta blocker carries a higher risk of new-onset diabetes.

cards.t: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers: side effects and cautions
q: why do ACE inhibitors cause a cough
who should not take ACE inhibitors or ARBs
what is ACE inhibitor angioedema
cards.x:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are used one or the other, never both. Side effects to know:
- Dry cough, which is bradykinin-mediated and occurs in up to about 1 in 5 patients. The fix is to switch to an ARB.
- Hyperkalemia (high potassium) and a rise in creatinine.
- Angioedema (swelling of the face, lips or throat), a bradykinin-mediated class effect that is 2 to 4 times more common in Black patients. An ARB is usually substituted.

Avoid them in pregnancy and in bilateral renal artery stenosis. After angioedema from an ACE inhibitor, do not give an ACE inhibitor again; an ARB can be used with caution.

cards.t: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) and their side effects
q: what are the side effects of amlodipine
why does amlodipine cause ankle swelling
can a diuretic fix calcium channel blocker edema
cards.x: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as amlodipine, are the third first-line class. Their classic side effect is dependent ankle edema (swelling of the lower legs), which is the most common one. It happens because the drug dilates blood vessels, so a diuretic does not fix it. Other effects are flushing, headache and gingival enlargement (overgrown gums).

cards.t: Antihypertensive combinations to avoid
q: why can't you combine an ACE inhibitor and an ARB
why avoid a beta blocker with verapamil or diltiazem
which drug combinations are contraindicated in hypertension
cards.x:
Two combinations are avoided outright.
- Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor plus angiotensin receptor blocker: dual blockade raises the risk of hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury with no additional benefit.
- Beta blocker plus verapamil or diltiazem: both slow the sinus node and the atrioventricular node, so the risk is severe bradycardia (a very slow heart rate) and heart block.

Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil and diltiazem) are also avoided where the ejection fraction is already reduced.

cards.t: Treating resistant hypertension, step by step
q: what is the fourth drug for resistant hypertension
how do you treat resistant hypertension
when do you refer for resistant hypertension
cards.x:
Once the look-alikes are excluded, treating resistant hypertension is a stepwise climb.
- Optimize the diuretic first: chlorthalidone is preferred, with the class matched to kidney function. An inadequate diuretic is a common reason the other two agents appear to fail.
- Titrate the renin-angiotensin blocker and the dihydropyridine to maximally tolerated doses.
- Add spironolactone, the most evidence-supported fourth agent, if filtration rate and potassium allow.
- Beyond that, choose by physiology and comorbidity: beta blockade, hydralazine (needs combination therapy because of reflex tachycardia, a reflex speeding of the heart, and fluid retention), or a central alpha-2 agonist such as clonidine (sedation, dry mouth, and rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal).
- Refer truly difficult cases to a hypertension specialist.

cards.t: Why blood pressure is lowered slowly in a hypertensive emergency
k: how fast to lower blood pressure
q: how fast should blood pressure be lowered in a hypertensive emergency
why not lower blood pressure quickly to normal
what are the exceptions to gradual lowering
cards.x:
In a hypertensive emergency the pressure is brought down in stages, not straight to normal. Lower the mean arterial pressure by no more than about 20 to 25% in the first hour, then toward roughly 160/100 to 110 over two to six hours, with gradual normalization over a day or two.

Why not faster? Autoregulation, the way organs protect their own blood supply, has adapted to the higher pressure: the organs have reset the range over which they protect their perfusion. Return the pressure to normal too quickly and they are underperfused at a value that would be safe in anyone else, causing ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.

The exceptions to this approach are aortic dissection and some stroke syndromes. Acute stroke follows its own protocol.

cards.t: Choosing blood pressure drugs in adults and in Black adults
k: thiazide or calcium channel blocker Black adults
q: which antihypertensive works best in Black adults
who responds better to ACE inhibitors
why is ACE inhibitor monotherapy less effective in some patients
cards.x:
The best drug depends partly on the patient. In adults, younger or salt-restricted patients often respond better to angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, while high salt intake favors a diuretic response.

In Black adults without heart failure or chronic kidney disease, a thiazide diuretic or a calcium channel blocker is used, often as an initial combination. The reason is a greater blood pressure response to those drugs and less efficacy with ACE inhibitor monotherapy. Angioedema from ACE inhibitors is also 2 to 4 times more common in Black patients; an angiotensin receptor blocker can usually be substituted.

cards.t: Blood pressure drugs in pregnancy
q: which blood pressure drugs are safe in pregnancy
why avoid ACE inhibitors in pregnancy
what is used for hypertension when planning pregnancy
cards.x: In pregnancy, or when planning one, the blood pressure drugs to use are labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are avoided because they are teratogenic, meaning they can cause birth defects.

cards.t: Hypertension in older adults: orthostatic checks and thiazide caution
q: what should you check in older adults with hypertension
how is orthostatic hypotension defined
why be careful with thiazides in older patients
cards.x:
Hypertension becomes far more common with age, reaching 71.6% at age 60 and over, so a few cautions matter in older adults. Check standing blood pressure: orthostatic hypotension is a fall of at least 20 systolic or at least 10 diastolic within 3 minutes of standing.

Watch volume status on a thiazide-type diuretic, especially in older adults, and use a thiazide with caution at 65 and over, particularly in women or with low-normal sodium or hyponatremia. Check sodium 1 to 2 weeks after starting it or increasing the dose.

If a narrowed kidney artery is the cause, atherosclerotic renovascular disease is the type that predominates in older patients with established vascular disease.

cards.t: Hypotension: what it is and why 'normal' depends on the patient
q: what is hypotension
what is relative hypotension
why does age matter when judging blood pressure
cards.x:
Hypotension is a decrease in systemic blood pressure below the normal level, and the catch is that normal depends on the patient. Blood pressure norms change with age, so a reading that is normal for an adult may be abnormal for an infant or child, and the reverse. Consider comorbidities, and consider relative hypotension, meaning a pressure well below the patient's own usual reading. Each reading is also only a snapshot in time.

When hypotension is symptomatic, low peripheral resistance or low cardiac output lowers the pressure until blood flow to the brain falls and consciousness is briefly lost. That brief loss of consciousness is syncope.

cards.t: Syncope versus near-syncope (presyncope)
q: what is syncope
what is the difference between syncope and near-syncope
how does syncope differ from a seizure
cards.x:
Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness with an inability to maintain postural tone, followed by spontaneous recovery, meaning full recovery. It is brief and self-limited, which helps separate it from a seizure.

Near-syncope, also called presyncope, is the set of symptoms that come before a faint: dizziness, lightheadedness and tunnel vision. So near-syncope is the warning and syncope is the faint itself, which adds the loss of consciousness and posture.

cards.t: The three main groups of syncope: orthostatic, reflex and cardiogenic
q: what are the main causes of syncope
how do orthostatic, reflex and cardiogenic syncope differ
what mechanism lies behind each type of syncope
cards.x:
The most common causes of syncope fall into three groups, each with its own mechanism.
- Orthostatic (neurogenic and non-neurogenic): autonomic failure (primary, secondary or drug-induced) lowers peripheral resistance, or volume depletion or venous pooling lowers venous return and cardiac output.
- Reflex (situational and vasovagal): an inappropriate reflex, which can be vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory or mixed.
- Cardiogenic (arrhythmia, structural and vascular): low cardiac output.

In every group, the final common step is the same: not enough blood reaches the brain for a moment.

cards.t: Non-hypotensive causes of syncope, and features that argue against a seizure
k: causes of fainting not from low blood pressure
q: what causes syncope other than hypotension
how do you tell syncope from a seizure
is POTS a cause of syncope
cards.x:
Not every faint comes from low pressure. The non-hypotensive causes of syncope are hypoglycemia, seizure, toxic exposure or overdose, electrolyte imbalance, hypoxia (for example from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or congestive heart failure), anxiety, anemia, and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome.

One look-alike is seizure. Features that argue against a seizure are no tonic-clonic activity, no tongue biting, no incontinence, no prolonged (postictal) confusion, and rapid spontaneous recovery.

cards.t: Acute versus chronic hypotension and their causes
q: what is the difference between acute and chronic hypotension
what causes acute hypotension
what causes chronic hypotension
cards.x:
Acute and chronic hypotension differ in onset, symptoms and cause.
- Acute: sudden onset, usually symptomatic, usually from a specific trigger. Examples are toxic exposure or overdose, including medication-mediated; and infection (bacteremia, sepsis, septic shock), which gives long-lasting acute hypotension.
- Chronic: waxes and wanes, is intermittently symptomatic, and the underlying cause may be unavoidable. The example is cardiogenic: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or cardiomyopathy.

So think of acute as 'something just happened' and chronic as 'something ongoing that comes and goes'.

cards.t: Diagnostic criteria for orthostatic hypotension
q: how is orthostatic hypotension diagnosed
how far does blood pressure have to fall on standing
do you need all three orthostatic criteria
cards.x:
Orthostatic hypotension is diagnosed from blood pressure taken lying down and again on standing. Any one of these within 3 minutes of standing is enough:
- Systolic pressure falls by at least 20 mmHg.
- Diastolic pressure falls by at least 10 mmHg.
- With an elevated baseline or supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat), systolic pressure falls by more than 30 mmHg.

You do not need all three; one is enough. Note the higher bar in the third criterion: when the patient starts out with supine hypertension, many use a systolic fall of 30 or more instead of 20. History is the most important part of working out the source of orthostatic syncope, or of referring to the right specialty to confirm it.

cards.t: First-line care for orthostatic syncope
q: how do you manage orthostatic syncope
why do slow position changes help
what is first-line treatment for orthostatic hypotension
cards.x:
First-line care for orthostatic syncope has two parts. The first is slow positional changes, with a pause sitting before standing, which limits the pressure drop on standing. The second is treating the underlying cause (treat the real diagnosis), which addresses the problem behind the low pressure. Drugs come in when these are not enough.

Understanding why the pressure falls helps patients follow the advice, so counseling is part of the treatment.

cards.t: Neurogenic versus non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: the heart rate tell
q: how do you tell neurogenic from non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
what does heart rate tell you in orthostatic hypotension
what causes each type of orthostatic hypotension
cards.x:
Both forms meet the same pressure criteria, so the heart rate decides. A cardiac response means the autonomic system is intact, so the problem is non-neurogenic. Little or no heart rate rise means the sympathetic reflex is not compensating, which favors neurogenic.
- Non-neurogenic: typical cause volume loss or medications; significant heart rate increase; volume depletion often present; autonomic symptoms usually absent. Examples: diarrhea, hemorrhage, diuretics.
- Neurogenic: typical cause autonomic failure; minimal heart rate increase; volume depletion usually absent; autonomic symptoms often present. Examples: diabetes, Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy.

Worked example: supine 138/78 with heart rate 68, standing 108/64 with heart rate 92 shows an intact response, so non-neurogenic. Supine 142/82 with heart rate 72, standing 108/66 with heart rate 76 shows pressure falling without a compensatory rise, so neurogenic.

cards.t: What the tests in a syncope work-up rule out
q: what tests are done for syncope
what does a normal glucose or electrocardiogram rule out in syncope
why check a blood count and metabolic panel in syncope
cards.x:
After a faint, the history comes first, and then simple tests each rule something out.
- A normal blood glucose rules out hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause.
- An unremarkable blood count and metabolic panel lower suspicion of infection or a metabolic cause.
- No neurologic deficit on exam lowers suspicion of a stroke.
- A normal electrocardiogram lowers suspicion of a dysrhythmia.

cards.t: Vasovagal syncope, the common faint
q: what is vasovagal syncope
what triggers vasovagal syncope
what is the mechanism of vasovagal syncope
cards.x:
Vasovagal syncope, the common faint, is reflex syncope triggered by emotional stress, fear, pain, heat exposure or standing for a long time. It is the most common type, most often in young women. Its cause is unclear, with a possible genetic predisposition.

The chain of events: parasympathetic outflow rises briefly while the sympathetic system is inhibited. That produces bradycardia (a slow heart rate) and vasodilation, so cardiac output falls, systolic pressure drops and cerebral blood flow falls below the limits of autoregulation.

The typical story is a prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating and lightheadedness, then a brief faint with rapid recovery, and normal findings afterward including normal standing readings. A clue to the diagnosis is the trigger plus that prodrome.

cards.t: Situational (micturition) syncope
q: what is situational syncope
what is micturition syncope
what are the triggers and risk factors for micturition syncope
cards.x:
Situational syncope is reflex syncope triggered by a bodily function or physical action, such as coughing, sneezing or urinating (micturition). In micturition syncope, an exaggerated autonomic reflex raises vagal activity and lowers sympathetic vascular tone.

One example is a 76-year-old man who faints at night while urinating standing up after rising abruptly from bed. Contributors were alcohol, relative dehydration, and an alpha-1 blocker (tamsulosin) taken with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (lisinopril). He had a brief prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating and lightheadedness ('swimmy' head) and then rapid recovery, with normal vital signs, examination, glucose and electrocardiogram afterward.

Treatment is to reduce or remove the trigger, with trigger avoidance and safety precautions.

cards.t: Diagnosing and treating reflex syncope: history, a log and trigger avoidance
q: how is reflex syncope diagnosed
why keep a log of fainting episodes
how do you treat reflex syncope
cards.x:
Reflex syncope is diagnosed mainly from the history, summed up as 'history, history, history'. The patient keeps a log of the pattern and frequency of episodes, which supports a history-based diagnosis and helps identify the triggers to avoid. If the cause is still unclear, refer to the right specialty.

Treatment is trigger avoidance: reduce or remove the trigger. When a trigger cannot be avoided, such as blood draws, take safety precautions during it.

cards.t: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS)
q: what is POTS
how is POTS diagnosed
how does POTS differ from orthostatic hypotension
how is POTS treated
cards.x:
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is a sustained rise in heart rate of 30 or more beats per minute within 10 minutes of standing, without orthostatic hypotension (an older definition also counts a rate above 120), with symptoms that usually improve lying down. In adolescents the threshold is an increase of 40. It occurs at ages 15 to 50, usually in women more than men, and is associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Symptoms are tachycardia with or without lightheadedness, dizziness, fainting and palpitations on standing.

Quick way to tell it from orthostatic hypotension: orthostatic hypotension is a pressure fall within 3 minutes, while this syndrome is a heart rate rise within 10 minutes.

Treatment starts with more water and salt and other nondrug measures. Fludrocortisone, which expands blood volume, is one drug option, but it is avoided in congestive heart failure because it causes salt and water retention.

cards.t: The tilt-table test: what a positive or negative result means
q: what does a negative tilt-table test mean
how sensitive is the tilt-table test
why can a tilt-table test be negative in POTS
cards.x: The tilt-table test is used to check for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome. It has a sensitivity of about 40% and a specificity above 80%. Sensitivity of 40% means many patients with the syndrome test negative, so a negative result tells you almost nothing and does not exclude it. Specificity above 80% means a positive result carries more weight.

cards.t: Cardiogenic syncope: arrhythmic, structural and vascular causes
q: what is cardiogenic syncope
how does cardiogenic syncope present
how do you work up cardiogenic syncope
cards.x:
Cardiogenic syncope is syncope from a cardiac cause, with or without hypotension. The common thread is low cardiac output. It comes in three types:
- Arrhythmia: atrial fibrillation, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, premature ventricular contractions and ventricular tachycardia, QT syndromes and heart blocks.
- Structural: myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy, heart failure and valve disease.
- Vascular: peripheral vascular disease, dissection, aneurysm, stroke and pulmonary embolism.

It gives itself away by an abrupt witnessed collapse with minimal or no prodrome (no nausea, sweating or warmth beforehand), sometimes after palpitations, in someone with heart disease.

Work-up: for arrhythmia, an electrocardiogram, monitoring and a stress test; for structural causes, an echocardiogram or stress echocardiogram; for vascular causes, emergent testing in the emergency department. Cardiology is consulted in each.

cards.t: Treating hypotension and syncope: remove the cause, educate, then match the drug
q: how do you treat syncope
what is the first step in treating iatrogenic hypotension
why is patient education important in syncope
cards.x:
Treatment starts by trying to remove the offending agent or trigger, matched to the cause:
- Iatrogenic (caused by treatment): reduce or remove the medication.
- Reflex: reduce or remove the trigger.
- Orthostasis: treat the underlying condition.

Alongside that comes patient education, and understanding is the key to compliance. Once patients know why the pressure falls on standing, slow position changes make sense and are followed, so education is often the most important part. Drugs are then matched to the condition.

cards.t: Drugs for hypotension and syncope: which drug for which condition
q: which drug is used for neurogenic syncope
when is fludrocortisone used and avoided
when is droxidopa used
which vasopressors are for the emergency department only
cards.x:
Match the drug to the condition:
- Midodrine: for neurogenic syncope. Avoid it with supine hypertension, severe heart disease or chronic kidney disease.
- Fludrocortisone: raises blood volume, so it is used in postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. It causes salt and water retention, so avoid it in congestive heart failure.
- Droxidopa: its efficacy is mild and it is usually an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone. Like midodrine, it can cause or worsen supine hypertension, so it needs the same caution.
- Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin: emergency department and intensive care only.

cards.t: Four syncope cases at a glance and how to tell them apart
q: how do you tell the types of syncope apart from a case
what clues point to cardiogenic syncope
what clues point to neurogenic versus volume-depletion orthostatic hypotension
cards.x:
Four cases show how the clues sort the types of syncope.
- A 76-year-old man faints while voiding standing at 2 a.m., after alcohol and little water, taking tamsulosin with lisinopril. He had a warm, nauseated, sweaty prodrome, and vitals, examination, glucose and electrocardiogram were normal. This is micturition syncope, a reflex (situational) type.
- A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes faints after standing and has reduced sensation in both feet. Pressure falls 142/82 to 108/66 with heart rate 72 to 76. This is neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
- A 72-year-old man with diarrhea, poor intake and a recent hydrochlorothiazide increase has dry mucous membranes and 138/78 to 108/64 with heart rate 68 to 92. This is intravascular volume depletion, non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
- A 76-year-old man with a prior heart attack and an ejection fraction of 30% collapses abruptly with no prodrome after a racing heart; he has 88/54, heart rate 148 and a rapid regular rhythm. This is ventricular tachycardia that is still going (sustained and unstable), causing cardiogenic syncope.

cards.t: A memory aid for the lipoproteins: the city and its trucks
q: how can I remember what each lipoprotein does
why is HDL called garbage trucks
what is the lipoprotein analogy
cards.x:
Here is one picture to hang the lipoprotein roles on. Triglyceride is fuel and cholesterol is building material. Every lipoprotein is a sealed truck carrying them, with apolipoproteins as badges on the outside. The liver is the central depot, the intestines are the port where dietary cargo arrives, and bile is the sewer.
- Chylomicron: a fuel barge from the port, only after a fatty meal.
- Very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL): the depot's outbound fuel tanker. Intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL) is the tanker after its drop-off.
- Low-density lipoprotein (LDL): the building-material delivery truck. Too many on the road is the city's biggest hazard.
- High-density lipoprotein (HDL): the garbage trucks, collecting excess cholesterol and hauling it back to the depot and down the bile sewer.
- Lipoprotein(a): a delivery truck towing an extra armored trailer.

Use the story to remember who does what, and answer questions about facts from the facts themselves.

cards.t: Lipoproteins: what they are and the five types by density
k: how fats travel in the blood
q: what is a lipoprotein
what are the types of lipoproteins
how are lipoproteins classified
cards.x:
Lipoproteins are the particles that carry cholesterol, triglyceride and fat-soluble vitamins through plasma, interstitial fluid and lymph. Each has a core of hydrophobic (water-avoiding) lipids, namely triglyceride and cholesteryl esters, inside a shell of hydrophilic (water-friendly) lipids, namely phospholipids and unesterified cholesterol. Proteins called apolipoproteins are built in as well.

They are classified by density into five types, from least to most dense: chylomicrons, very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL), low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and high-density lipoprotein (HDL). A sixth particle, lipoprotein(a), looks like LDL with an extra protein.

cards.t: Chylomicrons, VLDL and IDL
q: what do chylomicrons do
what is VLDL
what is IDL and where does it come from
cards.x:
Chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) carry triglyceride, and intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL) is what is left of VLDL.
- Chylomicrons are the least dense. They are in the blood after fatty food. Lipoprotein lipase strips off their triglyceride, which goes to muscle and fat cells for energy or storage, and the leftover chylomicron remnants are taken up by the liver. Extremely high levels lead to eruptive xanthomas.
- VLDL is denser than chylomicrons. It is mainly triglyceride with some cholesterol, and it transfers triglyceride to cells. Increased VLDL raises risk.
- IDL has intermediate density. It is what remains of VLDL: VLDL remnants become IDL.

cards.t: LDL: the 'bad' cholesterol
q: what is LDL
why is LDL called bad cholesterol
what does LDL do in the body
cards.x:
Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is mostly cholesterol, and its job is to provide cholesterol for the cells' needs. It transports cholesterol and is called the 'bad' cholesterol because it carries the highest risk: increased levels put patients at risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

Quick way to keep LDL and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) straight: LDL delivers cholesterol out to the cells and raises risk, while HDL carries excess cholesterol back to the liver and lowers risk.

cards.t: HDL: the 'good' cholesterol and reverse cholesterol transport
q: what does HDL do
what is reverse cholesterol transport
why is HDL called good cholesterol
cards.x: High-density lipoprotein (HDL) is the most dense and smallest lipoprotein, made mainly of apoproteins and cholesterol, and it is made in the liver and intestines. Its job is reverse cholesterol transport: it carries excess cholesterol from the periphery (body tissues) back to the liver for excretion into bile. That is why it is called the 'good' cholesterol, and why it is linked to decreased risk. HDL can be increased with exercise.

cards.t: Lipoprotein(a): what it is and why elevated levels matter
q: what is lipoprotein(a)
why does an elevated lipoprotein(a) matter
how is elevated lipoprotein(a) managed
cards.x:
Lipoprotein(a) is similar to low-density lipoprotein (LDL) in lipid and protein composition, but it carries apolipoprotein(a) in addition to apolipoprotein B-100. It is cleared by the liver.

Its importance is that it is a causal and independent risk factor for atherosclerotic disease. 'Independent' means it adds risk by itself, apart from the usual lipid numbers. So when it is elevated, the patient needs aggressive therapy to decrease LDL.

cards.t: Apolipoproteins: A-I, B-48, B-100, C, E and (a)
q: what do apolipoproteins do
which apolipoprotein is on which lipoprotein
what is the difference between B-48 and B-100
cards.x:
Apolipoproteins give lipoproteins their structure, activate enzymes of lipoprotein metabolism, and act as ligands (docking signals) for receptors on cells.
- B is the major structural protein of chylomicrons, very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), intermediate-density lipoprotein (IDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL). It is not present in high-density lipoprotein (HDL).
- B-48 is made in the intestines and sits on chylomicrons.
- B-100 is made in the liver and sits on VLDL, IDL, LDL and lipoprotein(a); it is one of the largest human proteins.
- A-I is made in the liver and intestines and is the major structural protein of HDL, on all HDL particles. A-II is the second most abundant, on two-thirds of HDL particles.
- C, C-III and A-V regulate triglyceride metabolism.
- E is critical in triglyceride clearance, and its mutation causes familial dysbetalipoproteinemia.
- (a) forms lipoprotein(a).

cards.t: Why lipids matter: coronary heart disease, LDL and the Framingham study
k: coronary heart disease leading cause of death
q: why does cholesterol matter
what did the Framingham Heart Study show
is LDL or triglyceride the better predictor of heart disease
cards.x:
Coronary heart disease is the leading cause of death in men and women in the United States, and diagnosing and treating dyslipidemia lowers that risk. More than $200 billion a year is spent on it, driven by poorly implemented prevention and uncontrolled risk factors.

The risk of atherosclerosis is directly related to raised serum cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is a better predictor of heart disease than triglyceride.

The Framingham Heart Study began in 1948 with 5,209 men and women aged 30 to 62 who had no cardiovascular disease. It linked raised cholesterol to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Its major risk factors were high blood pressure, high serum cholesterol, smoking, obesity, diabetes and physical inactivity.

cards.t: Major risk factors for coronary disease, with HDL as a negative one
k: risk factors for coronary heart disease
q: what are the major risk factors for coronary heart disease
what counts as premature family history
what does a negative risk factor mean
cards.x:
The modified list of major risk factors counts:
- Cigarette smoking.
- Hypertension: 140/90 or higher, or on antihypertensive medication.
- Low high-density lipoprotein (HDL): under 40 mg/dL.
- Family history of premature coronary disease: a male first-degree relative under 55, or a female first-degree relative under 65.
- Age: men 45 and older, women 55 and older.

HDL is special. An HDL of 60 or more is a 'negative' risk factor, which removes one risk factor from the count.

cards.t: Coronary heart disease risk equivalents
q: what are coronary heart disease risk equivalents
is diabetes a coronary risk equivalent
which conditions carry the same risk as known coronary disease
cards.x:
Coronary heart disease risk equivalents are conditions treated as carrying the same risk as established coronary disease. The list below begins with that established disease itself (myocardial infarction, angina, coronary interventions) and then gives the equivalents:
- Myocardial infarction.
- Angina, especially unstable angina.
- Coronary interventions.
- Peripheral arterial disease.
- Abdominal aortic aneurysm.
- Symptomatic carotid disease (stroke or transient ischemic attack).
- Diabetes mellitus.
- Multiple risk factors with a Framingham risk above 20%.

This idea is also why the Adult Treatment Panel III modification of the Framingham score removed diabetes from its algorithm: diabetes was already treated as a coronary risk equivalent.

cards.t: Estimating risk: the Framingham score and the Pooled Cohort Equation
q: what is the Pooled Cohort Equation
what is the Framingham risk score
who is the Pooled Cohort Equation used for
cards.x:
Risk estimators put a person's numbers into an equation to get a 10-year risk. Most use age, sex, total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL), systolic pressure, diabetes and current smoking, and the advice is to use one validated in a population like the patient.
- Framingham estimates 10-year coronary risk. It was the primary United States score from 2002 to 2013. The 2002 Adult Treatment Panel III modification removed diabetes from the algorithm because diabetes was treated as a coronary risk equivalent.
- The Pooled Cohort Equation, recommended from 2013, estimates 10-year primary risk of atherosclerotic disease in people aged 40 to 79 without pre-existing cardiovascular disease. It has separate calculators for White and Black individuals.

cards.t: The 2018 ten-year risk categories and what each means for a statin
q: what are the 10-year risk categories for statin decisions
what risk level calls for a moderate-intensity statin
what do you do at borderline risk
cards.x:
The 2018 risk categories pick the candidates for statin therapy, based on the estimated 10-year risk:
- Under 5%: low. A risk discussion emphasizing lifestyle.
- 5% to under 7.5%: borderline. If risk enhancers are present, discuss a moderate-intensity statin.
- 7.5% to under 20%: intermediate. If risk and enhancers favor it, use a moderate-intensity statin to lower low-density lipoprotein (LDL) by 30 to 49%.
- 20% or higher: high. A statin to lower LDL by 50% or more.

At borderline risk, risk enhancers such as premature menopause before age 40 prompt a risk discussion about a moderate-intensity statin.

cards.t: Major atherosclerotic events and what makes someone 'very high risk'
k: symptomatic peripheral arterial disease ankle-brachial index
q: what is very high risk atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
what counts as a major ASCVD event
what high-risk conditions add to a major event
cards.x:
The major atherosclerotic events are a recent acute coronary syndrome (within 12 months), a history of myocardial infarction, a history of ischemic stroke, and symptomatic peripheral arterial disease (claudication with an ankle-brachial index under 0.85, or revascularization or amputation).

Very high risk means multiple major events, or one major event plus multiple high-risk conditions. The high-risk conditions are age 65 or older, heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, prior bypass or percutaneous coronary intervention, diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, current smoking, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) of 100 or more despite maximal statin and ezetimibe, and congestive heart failure.

cards.t: Physical signs of lipid disorders: xanthomas, xanthelasma and corneal arcus
q: what are xanthomas
which xanthoma goes with which lipid problem
what does corneal arcus before age 40 mean
cards.x:
Most patients with dyslipidemia have no specific signs, but these findings usually point to an underlying genetic condition:
- Eruptive xanthomas: clusters of small yellowish-white papules on the back, buttocks and extensor surfaces. They go with extremely high chylomicrons or VLDL (triglyceride).
- Tendinous xanthomas: firm nodules on the Achilles, patellar and back-of-hand tendons. They go with raised low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and familial hypercholesterolemia.
- Tuberous xanthomas: large firm nodules over the elbows, buttocks and thighs. A genetic condition.
- Xanthelasma: yellow plaques on the eyelids near the inner corners. A genetic condition.
- Corneal arcus: a white or gray ring around the cornea from cholesterol deposition. It is common in older adults (arcus senilis) but abnormal before age 40, and common in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
Premature coronary artery disease at ages 30 to 50 and pancreatitis also suggest a genetic condition.

cards.t: Lipid panel reference values for cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglyceride
q: what are the LDL cholesterol categories
what triglyceride level is very high
what counts as low HDL
cards.x:
The lipid panel is read against set bands, in mg/dL.
- Total cholesterol: under 200 desirable, 200 to 239 borderline high, over 240 high.
- Low-density lipoprotein (LDL): under 100 optimal, 100 to 129 near or above optimal, 130 to 159 borderline high, 160 to 189 high, over 190 very high.
- High-density lipoprotein (HDL): under 40 low, over 60 high.
- Triglyceride: under 150 normal, 150 to 199 borderline high, 200 to 499 high, over 500 very high.

Read the values as a decision, not just a table: untreated abnormal values predict higher cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, so a high number means asking whether to start treatment such as a statin.

cards.t: Dyslipidemia: definition, causes and first steps
q: what is dyslipidemia
what causes dyslipidemia
what is the first step in evaluating dyslipidemia
cards.x:
Dyslipidemia is a disorder of lipoprotein metabolism: lowered high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and/or raised total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), non-HDL cholesterol (all cholesterol except HDL) or triglyceride. Most patients have no signs or symptoms and are found from abnormal lab values. When present, the findings are xanthomas, corneal arcus, premature coronary disease (ages 30 to 50) and pancreatitis.

Causes are primary (genetic) or secondary. The primary ones are overproduction or defective clearance of triglyceride or LDL, or excessive clearance or underproduction of HDL; genetic types are the most common cause in children, and mixed dyslipidemia is the most common type in clinical practice. Secondary causes include a sedentary lifestyle with a diet high in carbohydrate and saturated or trans fat, diabetes, alcohol, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, obstructive liver disease and medications.

The critical first step is to work out which lipoproteins are raised or lowered. Rule out secondary causes, then primary causes, before starting a statin. Treatment has three parts: therapeutic lifestyle changes, drug therapy and a clinician-patient risk discussion, with LDL as the primary target.

cards.t: Severe hypertriglyceridemia: pattern, risks and treatment
q: what is severe hypertriglyceridemia
what is the risk of triglyceride above 500
how is triglyceride above 500 treated
cards.x:
Severe hypertriglyceridemia is triglyceride above 500 mg/dL, with raised total cholesterol and reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL), but usually no rise in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) or apolipoprotein B. The cause is impaired lipolysis, a problem breaking down triglyceride. It usually involves a polygenic tendency (many genes) combined with secondary factors such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, a high-carbohydrate diet, alcohol, chronic kidney disease, nephrotic syndrome and certain drugs. The danger is acute pancreatitis, and eruptive xanthomas may appear with extremely high chylomicrons or very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL).

At 500 or higher, rule out diabetes, chronic kidney disease, alcoholism, pregnancy and hypothyroidism before a statin. Treatment above 500 is a very low-fat diet (under 15% of calories from fat), weight management, physical activity and a fibrate, which lowers the pancreatitis risk.

cards.t: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
