q: what is familial chylomicronemia syndrome
what is lipemia retinalis
what are the signs of familial chylomicronemia syndrome
cards.x:
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome is a primary (genetic) disorder that causes severe hypertriglyceridemia: fasting triglyceride above 500 mg/dL and usually above 1000. It can present in childhood or adulthood, and it matters because of the risk of acute pancreatitis.

The clues are severe abdominal pain from acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas (small yellowish-white papule clusters on the back, buttocks and extensor arms and legs), and lipemia retinalis, an opalescent look to the retinal blood vessels on fundoscopy. The liver and spleen may be enlarged (hepatosplenomegaly).

A fasting triglyceride above 500, usually above 1000, with eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis or pancreatitis raises the suspicion; because most severe hypertriglyceridemia has other causes, genetic testing confirms the diagnosis. The plan starts with the general measures for triglyceride above 500: a very low-fat diet, weight management and activity. A fibrate is the usual add-on for severe hypertriglyceridemia, but it works poorly in this genetic syndrome, where strict fat restriction is the mainstay.

cards.t: Hypercholesterolemia (raised LDL): causes and approach
q: what is hypercholesterolemia
what is the treatment for LDL of 190 or higher
what should be ruled out when LDL is high
cards.x:
Hypercholesterolemia here means elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and the underlying problem is impaired hepatic uptake of LDL, with fewer or weaker LDL receptors. Anything that lowers receptor activity can cause it: a diet high in saturated and trans fat, hypothyroidism, estrogen deficiency and liver disorders. Cushing syndrome, nephrotic syndrome and glucocorticoids also raise LDL. There are usually no signs; it goes with premature atherosclerotic disease, and tendinous xanthomas may appear with high LDL.

When LDL is raised, rule out hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, primary biliary cirrhosis and anorexia nervosa, and screen for low thyroid. LDL is the primary target and statins come first. With LDL of 190 or higher, use a high-intensity statin without calculating risk, and add ezetimibe if LDL stays at 100 or higher.

cards.t: Familial hypercholesterolemia: homozygous versus heterozygous
q: what is familial hypercholesterolemia
what is the difference between homozygous and heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
how do I tell homozygous from heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
cards.x:
Familial hypercholesterolemia is passed down from parents, so family history matters. Both forms are a codominant mutation of the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor gene, which reduces clearance of LDL from the blood. In both, LDL is usually above 190 with a normal triglyceride, with tendon xanthomas and premature atherosclerotic disease.

The difference is the number of mutant alleles. Homozygous means two mutant alleles; heterozygous means one.

Quick way to tell them apart: a child with very high cholesterol (total about 400 or more) and xanthomas should make you think homozygous, confirmed by genetic testing (skin biopsy was the classic test). A 40-year-old with relatives who died young should make you think heterozygous, the far more common form, which is diagnosed mainly clinically with no single definitive test.

cards.t: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
q: what is homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
how is homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia treated
what is LDL apheresis
cards.x:
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia comes from two mutant low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor alleles. It is either receptor-negative (under 2% of normal receptor activity) or receptor-defective (2 to 25%). It is rare, classically quoted as about 1 in 1 million (newer estimates are closer to 1 in 300,000), and presents in childhood with a strong family history of raised lipids in parents and other first-degree relatives.

The picture is a child with cutaneous xanthomas (on the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, heels or buttocks), tendon xanthomas, a total cholesterol of about 400 to over 1000, and symptomatic atherosclerosis before puberty. The picture is clinical and is confirmed by genetic testing for LDL receptor gene mutations; the classic confirmation, a skin biopsy with LDL receptor activity, is rarely used now.

LDL apheresis, the elective removal of LDL particles like dialysis, is the treatment of choice. Most patients also need a high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe, with a PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) inhibitor if refractory. Niacin (nicotinic acid) was once added but is no longer recommended. Evinacumab is an adjunct (first approved from age 12, and in the United States now from age 5), and liver transplantation may help by providing LDL receptors.

Untreated, receptor-negative patients rarely survive past the second decade, and receptor-defective patients develop cardiovascular disease by 30.

cards.t: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
q: what is heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
how common is heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
how is heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia treated
cards.x:
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia comes from one mutant low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor allele, with LDL of 200 to 400 mg/dL. It affects about 1 in 250 people worldwide and accounts for up to 5% of premature myocardial infarctions (men under 55, women under 65). The cholesterol is high from birth and is usually found incidentally on routine screening, and there are usually no symptoms until premature coronary disease.

On exam, tendon xanthomas are present in about 75% (back of the hands, elbows, knees, mainly the Achilles), and corneal arcus is common. There is no definitive diagnostic test.

Treatment: aggressively reduce vascular risk factors (smoking, hypertension, diabetes), a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, and a high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe. Niacin (nicotinic acid) was once added but is no longer recommended. If refractory, add a PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) inhibitor, but do not jump straight to it. Inclisiran is an adjunct in adults.

cards.t: Mixed dyslipidemia (high triglyceride plus high LDL)
q: what is mixed dyslipidemia
what lab values define mixed dyslipidemia
what is the most common type of dyslipidemia
cards.x:
Mixed dyslipidemia means both triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) are raised: triglyceride above 150 mg/dL together with LDL above 130 or non-high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol above 160. It is the most common dyslipidemia seen in clinical practice. It comes from a genetic predisposition plus medical conditions and environmental factors, and it increases the risk of atherosclerotic disease.

For treatment, the guidance is the general order: LDL first, then triglyceride.

cards.t: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
q: what is familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
which xanthomas go with familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
what lab pattern defines familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
cards.x:
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia is a rare disorder that causes mixed dyslipidemia. Chylomicron and very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) remnants accumulate, so triglyceride and total cholesterol rise together, both to 250 to 500 mg/dL.

It is caused by an apolipoprotein E mutation, associated with two copies of one variant of apolipoprotein E, called apoE2. On its own that is not enough: it needs environmental and/or other genetic factors on top.

The distinctive skin finding is xanthomas of two kinds: palmar xanthomas (on the palms) and tuberoeruptive xanthomas. The long-term danger is accelerated atherosclerosis.

cards.t: Low HDL cholesterol: causes and how to raise it
q: what counts as low HDL
how do you raise HDL
which drug raises HDL the most
cards.x:
Low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) is an HDL under 40 mg/dL (the metabolic syndrome cutoff is under 40 for men and under 50 for women), while an HDL of 60 or more is a negative risk factor. It causes no symptoms but is a coronary risk factor, because reverse cholesterol transport is lost. Causes are genetic excessive clearance or underproduction of HDL, and anabolic steroids. Rule out diabetes, cigarette smoking and obesity.

It is best fixed by lifestyle:
- Stop smoking: up to a 10% rise.
- Weight loss: HDL rises about 1 mg/dL for every 6 pounds lost.
- Aerobic exercise: about a 5% rise, brisk for 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week.
- Healthier fats (olive, peanut, canola) with saturated fat under 7% of calories, and alcohol limited to a moderate amount.

Among drugs, niacin raises HDL most (15 to 35%), then fibrates (10 to 30%), statins (5 to 22%) and ezetimibe (8%).

cards.t: Metabolic syndrome: the five criteria
q: what are the criteria for metabolic syndrome
how many criteria are needed for metabolic syndrome
how is metabolic syndrome treated
cards.x:
Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed when any 3 of these 5 criteria are present:
- Waist over 40 inches (men) or over 35 inches (women).
- Triglyceride over 150 mg/dL.
- High-density lipoprotein (HDL) under 40 (men) or under 50 (women).
- Blood pressure above 130/85.
- Fasting glucose over 110 in the original criteria; current harmonized criteria use 100 or higher.

Note that obesity is measured by waist circumference (abdominal obesity), not body mass index. The syndrome is itself a risk enhancer for atherosclerotic disease. Lifestyle therapy is the primary intervention in all age groups.

cards.t: Secondary causes of high triglyceride and how each one acts
q: what secondary causes raise triglyceride
why does a high-carbohydrate diet raise triglyceride
which drugs raise triglyceride
cards.x:
Several everyday conditions and drugs push triglyceride up:
- High-carbohydrate diet: more hepatic secretion of very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) triglyceride, so more triglyceride.
- Obesity, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes: more hepatic VLDL, and insulin promotes hepatic fatty-acid synthesis.
- Excess alcohol: inhibits hepatic free-fatty-acid oxidation. Take an alcohol history when triglyceride is raised.
- Chronic kidney disease: VLDL and remnants accumulate because lipolysis and remnant clearance are reduced.
- Nephrotic syndrome: excess VLDL production, raising triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein (LDL).
- Estrogen: raises triglyceride, and also raises high-density lipoprotein (HDL). Monitor on birth control pills, new postmenopausal estrogen, or pregnancy.
- Glucocorticoids raise triglyceride and LDL; beta blockers, isotretinoin and bexarotene raise triglyceride.

cards.t: Secondary causes of high LDL or low HDL
q: what secondary causes raise LDL
why does hypothyroidism raise LDL
what lowers HDL
cards.x:
Several secondary causes of raised low-density lipoprotein (LDL) work by turning down the liver's LDL receptors, the docking sites that pull LDL out of the blood, so more LDL stays in the blood.
- Saturated and trans fat down-regulate hepatic LDL receptors.
- Hypothyroidism (low thyroid hormone) down-regulates them too, which is why patients with raised LDL are screened for low thyroid.
- Liver disorders down-regulate them as well.
- Cushing syndrome: glucocorticoid overproduction increases very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) synthesis and LDL.
- Nephrotic syndrome and glucocorticoids also raise LDL.

For high-density lipoprotein (HDL), anabolic steroids lower it, so they are a secondary cause of a low level, and stopping them addresses it.

cards.t: What to rule out before starting a statin
q: what should be ruled out before starting a statin
what conditions cause a high triglyceride of 500 or more
why look at the full lipid panel
cards.x:
Before a statin, look for secondary causes of the abnormal lipid pattern, then look for primary (genetic) ones.
- Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) raised: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, primary biliary cirrhosis, anorexia nervosa.
- Triglyceride 500 or higher: diabetes, chronic kidney disease, alcoholism, pregnancy, hypothyroidism.
- Low high-density lipoprotein (HDL): diabetes, smoking, obesity.

Primary causes still matter after that, because they change coronary risk, response to drugs, and the management of other family members. Review the full panel carefully: two patients with the same total cholesterol of 275 can have an HDL of 110 or an HDL of 25, which are very different situations.

cards.t: Why primary causes of dyslipidemia are sought and why families are screened
k: lipid screening in children family history
q: why look for primary causes of dyslipidemia
why screen family members for lipid disorders
at what age can lipid screening start in children
cards.x:
Even after secondary causes are excluded, primary (genetic) causes are sought. Identifying one influences the management of other family members, who may carry the same disorder, as well as the patient's own coronary risk and drug response.

That is also why lipid screening is appropriate for each child in an affected family. Elective screening is appropriate as young as 2 years with a family history of high cholesterol.

cards.t: Lipid screening: who to screen and when
q: when should lipid screening start
when are children screened for lipids
what decides whether to screen
cards.x:
The decision to screen rests on overall cardiovascular risk, independent of the lipid levels: age, sex, hypertension, smoking, family history of premature coronary disease (male relative under 55, female under 65) and diabetes. Screen all adults aged 20 and older.

For children, a non-fasting lipid profile is done once at ages 9 to 11 and again in late adolescence. Elective screening can start from age 2 when there is a family history of heart disease or high cholesterol.

cards.t: Do you need to fast for a lipid panel?
q: do you need to fast for a lipid panel
when is a fasting lipid sample needed
which lipid ratio predicts coronary risk best
cards.x:
Total cholesterol and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) need no fasting, and their ratio is the most efficient and cost-effective predictor of coronary risk.

Under the 2018 guideline, a non-fasting full panel (with the calculated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) value) is acceptable for routine screening. A fasting sample is needed when triglyceride is 400 mg/dL or more.

cards.t: Risk enhancers that favor starting a statin
q: what are the risk enhancers for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
when do risk enhancers matter
what laboratory findings count as risk enhancers
cards.x:
Risk enhancers are extra factors that tip the decision toward a statin when the 10-year risk is borderline or intermediate. They are:
- Family history of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
- Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) persistently 160 or higher.
- Metabolic syndrome.
- Chronic kidney disease.
- Preeclampsia, or premature menopause (before age 40).
- Inflammatory disease (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, human immunodeficiency virus infection).
- South Asian ancestry.
- Triglyceride persistently 175 or higher.
- If measured: apolipoprotein B of 130 or higher, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of 2.0 or higher, ankle-brachial index under 0.9, or lipoprotein(a) of 50 mg/dL or higher.

cards.t: Order of treatment in dyslipidemia: LDL first, then triglyceride
q: what is the primary target of cholesterol-lowering therapy
when do you treat high triglyceride
when is a fibrate used for triglyceride
cards.x:
Treatment has three parts: therapeutic lifestyle changes, drug therapy and a clinician-patient risk discussion. The order is to address low-density lipoprotein (LDL) first, then triglyceride, then add adjunctive therapy on top. The primary target of cholesterol-lowering therapy is elevated LDL.

A moderately raised triglyceride (about 175 to 499 mg/dL) is handled with lifestyle, a search for secondary causes (diabetes, alcohol, kidney disease, hypothyroidism and drugs) and statin intensity. A fibrate, along with a very low-fat diet, is reserved for a triglyceride of 500 or more, to prevent pancreatitis, and niacin is not added.

cards.t: Non-HDL cholesterol: what it is and when to use it
q: what is non-HDL cholesterol
how do you calculate non-HDL cholesterol
why use non-HDL cholesterol when triglyceride is high
cards.x:
Non-high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL cholesterol, which means all the cholesterol except what is in HDL. For example, a total cholesterol of 250 with an HDL of 40 gives a non-HDL of 210 mg/dL.

It is the measure to use when triglyceride is high: in hypertriglyceridemia, non-HDL cholesterol assesses heart-disease risk better than low-density lipoprotein (LDL) alone.

cards.t: Therapeutic lifestyle changes for dyslipidemia
q: what lifestyle changes lower cholesterol
how much saturated fat should be eaten with dyslipidemia
how much weight loss is the goal in dyslipidemia
cards.x:
Therapeutic lifestyle changes are part of treatment for everyone with dyslipidemia:
- Saturated fat under 7% of calories.
- More soluble fiber, 20 to 30 grams a day.
- Consider plant stanols or sterols (found in grains, vegetables, fruits, legumes, nuts and seeds).
- Lose 5 to 10% of initial weight; for someone at 200 pounds, that is 10 to 20 pounds.
- Moderate activity for 30 minutes a day, such as brisk walking, biking or active yoga.
- Stop smoking.

cards.t: Statins: effects, intensity levels, monitoring and follow-up
q: what defines high-intensity statin therapy
when do you recheck lipids after starting a statin
what do you monitor on a statin
cards.x:
Statins (atorvastatin, fluvastatin, lovastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin, pitavastatin) are the most effective drugs for lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL). They lower LDL by 25 to 63%, with the maximum effect in 4 to 6 weeks, and raise high-density lipoprotein (HDL) by 5 to 22%. Check a baseline liver enzyme, then repeat lipids to judge response. Check creatine kinase or liver tests only if symptoms (muscle pain or weakness, signs of liver problems) appear.

Statin intensity is defined by how far it drops LDL:
- High intensity: about 50% or more.
- Moderate intensity: 30% to under 50%.
- Low intensity: under 30%.

Follow-up: repeat the lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting or changing a statin, then every 3 to 12 months as needed. This checks adherence and response, and response is judged as the percentage fall in LDL from baseline.

cards.t: Which lipid drug does what: statins, fibrates, niacin, ezetimibe and more
q: which drug lowers triglyceride the most
which drug raises HDL the most
what do ezetimibe and bile acid sequestrants do
cards.x:
Match each drug to the lipid it moves:
- Statins: the best for lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL).
- Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate): the best for lowering triglyceride, down 20 to 50%, with high-density lipoprotein (HDL) up 10 to 30%.
- Niacin (nicotinic acid): the best for raising HDL (up 15 to 35%), and it also lowers triglyceride by 20 to 50% and LDL by 5 to 25%.
- Ezetimibe, a cholesterol absorption inhibitor: an adjunct for lowering LDL (down 18%), with HDL up 8% and triglyceride down 5 to 10%.
- Bile acid sequestrants (colestipol, cholestyramine, colesevelam): an adjunct for lowering LDL, down 15 to 30%.
- Fish oil: associated with lower coronary disease and coronary death, and may lower thrombotic stroke. Eat fish at least twice a week.

cards.t: PCSK9 inhibitors, bempedoic acid, inclisiran and evinacumab
q: when are PCSK9 inhibitors used
what is inclisiran used for
what is evinacumab used for
what comes first, ezetimibe or evolocumab
cards.x:
Newer lipid drugs have narrower jobs:
- PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab): injectable monoclonal antibodies, approved for familial hypercholesterolemia and expensive. They are used for refractory familial hypercholesterolemia, and for very high risk patients after a statin plus ezetimibe.
- Bempedoic acid: a newer oral drug that up-regulates low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors.
- Inclisiran: a subcutaneous injection used as an adjunct to a maximal statin in adults with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
- Evinacumab: an intravenous adjunct in homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (first approved from age 12, and in the United States now from age 5), lowering LDL and triglyceride.

The sequence matters. Add ezetimibe to a maximal statin before an injectable such as evolocumab; adding evolocumab first is out of sequence and less cost-effective.

cards.t: 2018 statin decisions when atherosclerotic disease is already present
k: very high risk ezetimibe then PCSK9
q: what statin do you use for clinical ASCVD
what do you add when very high risk patients stay above LDL 70
what about patients over 75 with ASCVD
cards.x:
For clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, the 2018 decisions are:
- Age 75 or younger: a high-intensity statin to lower low-density lipoprotein (LDL) by 50% or more, with a moderate-intensity statin if high intensity is not tolerated.
- Older than 75: starting a moderate- or high-intensity statin is reasonable, and continuing a high-intensity statin is reasonable.
- Very high risk with LDL still 70 or higher on a maximal statin: add ezetimibe first. Then add a PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) inhibitor if LDL stays at 70 or higher, which is less cost-effective.

cards.t: 2018 primary prevention statin decisions: LDL 190, diabetes, ages 40 to 75
q: when do you start a statin without calculating risk
what statin for a patient with diabetes
how do you decide on a statin for a patient aged 40 to 75
cards.x:
For people without cardiovascular disease, the 2018 decisions depend on who the patient is:
- Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) 190 or higher (severe primary hypercholesterolemia): a high-intensity statin without calculating 10-year risk. Add ezetimibe if LDL stays at 100 or higher.
- Diabetes, age 40 to 75, LDL 70 or higher: a moderate-intensity statin without calculating risk. High intensity is reasonable with multiple risk factors or at age 50 to 75.
- Age 40 to 75, no diabetes, LDL 70 to 189: a clinician-patient risk discussion first, then decide by 10-year risk. If a statin is indicated, lower LDL by 30% or more; at 20% risk or higher, lower it by 50% or more.

Lifestyle is emphasized for everyone, at every age.

cards.t: Coronary artery calcium score when the statin decision is uncertain
q: when is a coronary artery calcium score used
what does a calcium score of 0 mean for statins
what calcium score indicates a statin
cards.x:
A coronary artery calcium score is considered when the statin decision is uncertain, in adults aged 40 to 75 without diabetes, with low-density lipoprotein (LDL) of 70 to 189 and a 10-year risk of 7.5% to 19.9% (the intermediate range). How to read it:
- Score 0: a statin may be withheld or delayed, but not in smokers, in diabetes, or with a strong family history.
- Score 1 to 99: favors a statin, especially at age 55 or older.
- Score 100 or higher, or at or above the 75th percentile: a statin is indicated, unless the clinician-patient risk discussion defers it.

cards.t: Statins at ages 0 to 19, 20 to 39 and over 75
q: when do you start a statin in a child
what about statins in young adults
do all patients over 75 get a statin for primary prevention
cards.x:
Statin decisions change at the ends of the age range.
- Ages 0 to 19: lifestyle, with a statin once familial hypercholesterolemia is diagnosed.
- Ages 20 to 39: estimate lifetime risk to encourage lifestyle, and consider a statin with a family history of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) of 160 or higher.
- Over 75, primary prevention: clinical assessment and a risk discussion, not an automatic prescription.

cards.t: Murmur words: stenosis vs regurgitation, systolic vs diastolic
q: how do I tell stenosis from regurgitation by the murmur
which valve murmurs are systolic and which are diastolic
what do harsh, rumbling and blowing murmurs mean
cards.x:
The word used for the sound tells you the type of valve problem. A harsh or rumbling murmur means stenosis: a narrowed valve that blood has to push through, so there is abnormal forward flow and the chamber upstream works against pressure (pressure overload). A blowing murmur means regurgitation: a leaky valve that lets blood flow backward, so the chamber takes in extra blood (volume overload).

Timing then sorts the valves. The systolic murmurs are aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis and tricuspid regurgitation. The diastolic ones are aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, pulmonic regurgitation and tricuspid stenosis. A memory phrase for the diastolic group is "Arms rest because they are Pretty Tired": A-R-M-S for aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis, then P-R-T-S for pulmonic regurgitation and tricuspid stenosis.

Shortcut: only two conditions are both harsh and systolic, aortic stenosis and pulmonic stenosis, so a harsh systolic murmur is already a 50-50 choice.

cards.t: Heart sounds: first, second, third and fourth
q: what causes the first and second heart sounds
what is a third heart sound
when do you hear a fourth heart sound
cards.x:
The first heart sound (S1) is the atrioventricular valves closing, the tricuspid and mitral valves. The second heart sound (S2) is the semilunar valves closing, the pulmonic and aortic valves.

Two extra sounds can show up in diastole. The third heart sound (S3) comes early in diastole, just after the second sound, and means a large volume of blood is rushing into a dilated left ventricle, as in systolic heart failure. The fourth heart sound (S4) comes just before the first sound and means high pressure against a stiff, thickened (hypertrophied) left ventricle, as in diastolic heart failure.

Easy way to keep them apart: the third sound is the rush of blood into a stretched-out ventricle, and the fourth is the atrium pushing against a thick, stiff ventricle.

cards.t: Where to listen for each valve (A-P-E-T-M)
q: where do I listen for the aortic valve
what is Erb's point
what is the A-P-E-T-M order for listening to the heart
cards.x:
Five listening spots cover the valves, remembered in the order A-P-E-T-M:
- Aortic: second intercostal space (the gap between the second and third ribs), right sternal border, also called the right upper sternal border.
- Pulmonic: second intercostal space, left sternal border (left upper sternal border).
- Erb's point: third intercostal space, left sternal border.
- Tricuspid: fifth intercostal space, lower left sternal border.
- Mitral: the apex, which is the point of maximal impulse, in the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

cards.t: Breathing and murmur loudness (right on inspiration, left on expiration)
k: right sided murmurs louder with inspiration
q: why do right-sided murmurs get louder with inspiration
which murmurs get louder on inspiration
what does RILE stand for
cards.x:
Murmur loudness changes with breathing: right-sided murmurs are louder on inspiration (breathing in), and left-sided murmurs are louder on expiration (breathing out). The memory aid is R-I-L-E: Right Inspiration, Left Expiration.

The reason is blood flow. When you breathe in, pressure inside the chest becomes negative and more blood is drawn back toward the right side of the heart, so there is more right-sided preload and right-sided murmurs get louder. When you breathe out, pressure inside the chest rises and blood is forced out of the lungs into the left atrium, so there is more left-sided preload and left-sided murmurs get louder.

Louder with inspiration: tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis, tricuspid stenosis and pulmonic regurgitation. Louder with expiration: mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis.

A right-sided murmur that grows louder with inspiration is called the Carvallo sign.

cards.t: Aortic stenosis: what it is, causes and what it does to the heart
q: what is aortic stenosis
what causes aortic stenosis
why does aortic stenosis lead to heart failure
cards.x:
Aortic stenosis is obstruction of the left ventricle's outflow at the aortic valve, and it is the most common valvular disease. The most common cause over age 70 is degenerative wear and tear, tied to atherosclerosis risk factors such as high cholesterol, diabetes and smoking. Under age 70 the most common cause is a congenital bicuspid aortic valve, meaning a valve with two cusps instead of the normal three. Rheumatic heart disease and endocarditis can also cause it.

Here is what it does. The left ventricle has to push against a blocked exit, which is pressure overload. The muscle remodels and thickens evenly (concentric hypertrophy), the cavity stays small, and the stiff thick wall eventually produces diastolic heart failure with a preserved ejection fraction.

Progression is insidious because resting cardiac output holds up until late. Symptoms are rare until the valve opening narrows to about 1 square centimeter (normal is 3 to 4), usually at ages 60 to 80. About 80% of symptomatic patients are men.

cards.t: Aortic stenosis: severe criteria, the three symptoms and prognosis
q: what makes aortic stenosis severe
what are the classic symptoms of aortic stenosis and how long do patients survive
what is the prognosis of symptomatic aortic stenosis
cards.x:
Severe aortic stenosis is defined by three numbers: valve area under 1.0 square centimeter, mean pressure gradient across the valve over 40 mmHg, and jet velocity over 4.0 meters per second. A quick way to remember it is "1, 40 and 4".

The three classic symptoms each come with a survival time once they appear:
- Angina, usually with exertion: about 5 years.
- Syncope (fainting), usually with exertion: about 3 years.
- Congestive heart failure, shown as shortness of breath with exertion: about 2 years. This is the most common symptom and carries the worst prognosis.

The outlook changes sharply once symptoms start. Symptomatic aortic stenosis has a 75% mortality over 3 years, and about half of people with untreated severe disease are dead within two years.

cards.t: Aortic stenosis: the murmur and how maneuvers change it
q: what does the aortic stenosis murmur sound like
how do Valsalva, standing and squatting change the aortic stenosis murmur
how can you tell aortic stenosis is severe on exam
cards.x:
The aortic stenosis murmur is a harsh systolic ejection murmur that builds and fades (crescendo-decrescendo). It is heard best at the second right intercostal space, the right upper sternal border, and it spreads (radiates) to the carotid arteries.

Maneuvers change how much blood crosses the valve. The murmur gets softer with the Valsalva maneuver, standing and handgrip, because more afterload or less volume means less flow through the valve. It gets louder with squatting and with sitting forward, because more preload means more flow, and leaning forward also brings the valve closer to the chest wall.

One bedside clue to severe disease: feeling a forceful apex beat of the left ventricle at the same time as a delayed, weakened carotid pulse. It is a clinical way of separating moderate from severe stenosis.

cards.t: Aortic stenosis: how it is diagnosed and who gets referred
q: how is aortic stenosis diagnosed
what does the echocardiogram show in aortic stenosis
who needs a cardiology consult for aortic stenosis
cards.x:
Any symptom that suggests aortic stenosis, such as chest pressure or shortness of breath with exertion, or fainting, should lead to an echocardiogram. A transthoracic echocardiogram (done through the chest wall) shows thickened, calcified leaflets that open poorly in systole, and left ventricular hypertrophy in advanced disease. It is the test used for degenerative disease. A transesophageal echocardiogram is useful for congenital disease.

The electrocardiogram can show left ventricular hypertrophy in severe disease, but it has low sensitivity, so a normal tracing does not rule the problem out. Echocardiography confirms and grades the stenosis. Left heart catheterization is the invasive test, used when the echocardiogram is unclear or to image the coronary arteries before valve surgery.

Every patient with aortic stenosis on echocardiogram gets a cardiology consult to evaluate them and to set how often they need follow-up.

cards.t: Aortic stenosis: preload dependence, what to avoid and when to replace the valve
q: why are nitrates avoided in aortic stenosis
what is the treatment for aortic stenosis
why are aortic stenosis patients preload dependent
cards.x:
Medical treatment is not effective for aortic stenosis, so management is mostly about what to avoid. Preload is the amount of blood filling the ventricle before it squeezes, and these patients depend on it: anything that drops preload is risky. The rules are what to avoid:
- strenuous physical activity and competitive sports
- dehydration and low blood volume
- beta blockers and calcium channel blockers when there is hypertension
- nitrates when there is angina, because nitrates lower preload

Valve replacement is for severe disease (valve area under 1.0 square centimeter, mean gradient over 40 mmHg, jet velocity over 4.0 meters per second) with symptoms. It is also done without symptoms if the ejection fraction falls below 50%. Options are transcatheter aortic valve replacement, a mechanical valve (titanium and carbon, lifelong anticoagulation) or a biological valve (pig or cow tissue, no anticoagulation). Children and young adults get percutaneous aortic balloon valvuloplasty.

cards.t: Pressure overload vs volume overload: how the ventricle remodels
q: what is the difference between pressure overload and volume overload
why does aortic stenosis cause diastolic heart failure
why does regurgitation cause a dilated ventricle
cards.x:
A ventricle reshapes itself according to the kind of load it carries. Stenosis makes it push against a narrowed exit, which is pressure overload. The muscle thickens evenly (concentric hypertrophy), so the wall is thick and the cavity stays small. A thick, stiff wall fills poorly, which is diastolic heart failure with a preserved ejection fraction. Aortic stenosis is the example.

Regurgitation sends blood backward, so the chamber takes in extra blood with every beat, which is volume overload. The ventricle grows in a stretched-out way (eccentric hypertrophy) and dilates, so the cavity is enlarged, and the result is systolic heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction. Aortic regurgitation and mitral regurgitation are the examples.

This ties back to the murmur words: harsh or rumbling means stenosis and pressure overload; blowing means regurgitation and volume overload.

cards.t: How maneuvers change valve murmurs (Valsalva, standing, squatting, handgrip)
q: how do maneuvers change valve murmurs
which murmurs get louder with handgrip
does squatting make aortic stenosis louder
cards.x:
Maneuvers change how much blood reaches a valve or how hard the ventricle has to push, and each murmur follows.
- Valsalva softens the aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation and mitral stenosis murmurs.
- Standing softens the aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation and mitral regurgitation murmurs, because less blood returns to the heart.
- Squatting makes those same three louder. Sitting forward also makes aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation louder.
- Handgrip raises the resistance the ventricle pushes against. The aortic stenosis murmur gets softer, because less blood moves forward through the narrowed valve. The aortic regurgitation and mitral regurgitation murmurs get louder, because the extra resistance pushes more blood backward through the leaky valve.

For the right-sided murmurs, breathing is the maneuver that matters: inspiration makes them louder.

cards.t: Infective endocarditis as a cause of valve disease
q: which valves does infective endocarditis damage
how deadly is untreated endocarditis
what is the cause of tricuspid regurgitation in people who inject drugs
cards.x:
Infective endocarditis is infection of the inner lining of the heart, including the valves, and it can leave a valve narrowed or leaking.
- Aortic stenosis: endocarditis is an acquired cause. Among cases of endocarditis, 50% involve the mitral valve and 20% the aortic valve. Untreated endocarditis is almost always fatal.
- Aortic regurgitation: a valve cause, and a cause of the acute form, which brings cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema.
- Mitral regurgitation: an acute and a chronic cause.
- Tricuspid regurgitation: the primary cause is endocarditis in people who inject drugs. When endocarditis is on the tricuspid valve, it is usually from intravenous drug use.

cards.t: Aortic regurgitation: what it is, causes, acute vs chronic
q: what is aortic regurgitation
what causes aortic regurgitation
what is the difference between acute and chronic aortic regurgitation
cards.x:
Aortic regurgitation (also called aortic insufficiency) is incomplete closing of the aortic valve, so blood flows back into the left ventricle during diastole. The cause can be the valve itself or the aortic root it sits in, or both.
- Valve causes: congenital bicuspid valve, endocarditis, rheumatic fever, myxomatous (collagen) disease, trauma, syphilis and ankylosing spondylitis.
- Root causes: aortic dissection, cystic medial degeneration, Marfan syndrome, familial aneurysm, aortitis and hypertension.

The backflow is a volume load, so the left ventricle enlarges with eccentric hypertrophy and dilates. A dilated ventricle is systolic heart failure, with a reduced ejection fraction.

Acute aortic regurgitation (from infarction, endocarditis, dissection or trauma) causes cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema. Chronic disease stays silent for 10 to 15 years, then produces heart failure symptoms such as exertional dyspnea, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, plus anginal chest pain.

cards.t: Aortic regurgitation: the murmur, Corrigan's pulse and other signs
q: what is Corrigan's pulse
what does the aortic regurgitation murmur sound like
what is de Musset sign
cards.x:
The aortic regurgitation murmur is high-pitched, blowing and diastolic. It is heard at the third intercostal space along the left upper sternal border and radiates toward the apex. In chronic disease, a longer murmur generally means a worse leak. In acute severe regurgitation the murmur can be short and quiet even though the leak is severe. It gets softer with Valsalva and standing, and louder with squatting, sitting forward and handgrip.

The big leak through the valve also shows up in the pulses:
- Corrigan's pulse, also called a water hammer or collapsing pulse, is a very rapid upstroke followed by a rapid collapse.
- De Musset sign is head bobbing with each beat.
- Other findings include bounding pulses, a wide pulse pressure, thrills and a displaced point of maximal impulse.

Severe regurgitation means a regurgitant fraction of 50% or more, meaning half of the output goes back through the valve.

cards.t: Aortic regurgitation: diagnosis, treatment and referral
q: how is aortic regurgitation treated
what does the echocardiogram show in aortic regurgitation
what is the treatment for acute severe aortic regurgitation
cards.x:
Diagnosis: the echocardiogram determines the cause (such as aortic root dilation or dissection) and shows the anterior mitral leaflet fluttering during diastole where the leak jet strikes it. The electrocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy in chronic disease, but that is non-specific. Catheterization is definitive but not necessary.

Treatment depends on the situation:
- While the ejection fraction is preserved: medical afterload reduction (lowering the resistance the ventricle pumps against) with an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, or hydralazine.
- Acute severe disease: emergency valve replacement or repair, ideally within 24 hours. If surgery is delayed, stabilize in intensive care with intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside.
- Chronic disease with a mildly reduced or reduced ejection fraction, with or without symptoms: evaluate as a surgical candidate, because untreated survival is only about 2 to 3 years.

Any audible murmur gets a cardiology consult, and a dilated aortic root is monitored by a cardiologist.

cards.t: Mitral stenosis: what it is, causes and atrial fibrillation
q: what is mitral stenosis
what is the most common cause of mitral stenosis
why does mitral stenosis cause atrial fibrillation
cards.x:
Mitral stenosis is obstruction of the left atrium's outflow across the mitral valve. Rheumatic heart disease is the most common cause. About 80% of rheumatic mitral stenosis is in women, it is usually diagnosed about 20 years after the rheumatic fever, and it is rare in developed countries because rheumatic fever has become less common.

The chain of events: the leaflets become thickened and immobile, so the opening narrows. Blood backs up, and the left atrium grows larger and its pressure rises. A stretched left atrium tends to go into atrial fibrillation, and that raises the risk of clots (thromboembolism). Most patients whose left atrium is already affected will develop atrial fibrillation. The high pressure also spreads backward into the lungs, narrowing the lung vessels, raising pulmonary artery pressure and overloading the right ventricle, which ends in right-sided heart failure. Overall, the pattern is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

cards.t: Mitral stenosis: symptoms, hoarseness (Ortner syndrome) and the murmur
q: what is the murmur of mitral stenosis
what is Ortner syndrome
why does mitral stenosis cause hemoptysis and dysphagia
cards.x:
Symptoms start late, once the opening has narrowed to about a third of normal. First come left-sided heart failure symptoms: shortness of breath on exertion, cough, orthopnea (breathless lying flat), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (waking breathless) and fatigue. The enlarged left atrium adds three unusual ones:
- Hemoptysis (coughing blood), because the high left atrial pressure ruptures small bronchial vein connections.
- Hoarseness, called Ortner syndrome, because the big left atrium presses on the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
- Dysphagia (trouble swallowing), because the left atrium presses on the esophagus.

The murmur is a low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex that starts with an opening snap, a sound just after the second heart sound as the stiff valve opens. Listen with the bell of the stethoscope with the patient lying on the left side (left lateral decubitus). Like most murmurs, it gets softer with Valsalva.

cards.t: Mitral stenosis: severe criteria, tests and treatment
q: what defines severe mitral stenosis
how is mitral stenosis treated
what does the ECG show in mitral stenosis
cards.x:
The classic teaching is that severe mitral stenosis means a valve area under 1.0 square centimeter, a mean gradient over 10 mmHg and a peak velocity over 3.0 meters per second. Current guidelines call an area of 1.5 or less severe, and 1.0 or less very severe. The transthoracic echocardiogram shows a large left atrium and a stenotic valve. The electrocardiogram shows left atrial abnormality (in the P wave), often atrial fibrillation in severe disease, and right ventricular hypertrophy if pulmonary hypertension has developed. Catheterization is not necessary.

Treatment follows symptoms:
- Asymptomatic and in sinus rhythm: no therapy yet.
- Shortness of breath or orthopnea: loop diuretics such as furosemide or bumetanide.
- Severe disease with symptoms (dyspnea) or pulmonary hypertension: percutaneous balloon valvotomy; valve replacement for moderate symptoms or pulmonary hypertension.

Anyone with mitral stenosis on echocardiogram gets a cardiology consult. Any suggestive symptom, such as dyspnea on exertion or orthopnea, calls for an echocardiogram.

cards.t: Rheumatic heart disease and the valves it damages
k: group A strep and the heart
q: what is rheumatic heart disease
which valve problems does rheumatic fever cause
why is rheumatic heart disease rare in developed countries
cards.x:
Rheumatic heart disease is an autoimmune reaction to group A beta-hemolytic streptococci: the immune response to the infection ends up damaging the heart valves. Mitral stenosis from rheumatic fever has become rare in developed countries because rheumatic fever has become less common there.

The mitral valve is the best-known victim, since rheumatic heart disease is the most common cause of mitral stenosis. It also shows up elsewhere in the valve lists:
- Aortic stenosis: an acquired cause.
- Aortic regurgitation: one of the valve causes.
- Mitral regurgitation: an acute and a chronic cause.
- Tricuspid stenosis: the most common cause, usually alongside rheumatic mitral disease.

The details of rheumatic mitral stenosis (who gets it and when it is found) are on the mitral stenosis card.

cards.t: Mitral regurgitation: what it is, acute and chronic causes, and what it does
q: what causes mitral regurgitation
what is the difference between acute and chronic mitral regurgitation
how does mitral regurgitation lead to heart failure
cards.x:
Mitral regurgitation is incomplete closing of the mitral valve, so blood flows backward into the left atrium during systole.
- Acute causes: a heart attack with papillary muscle rupture, infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever, rupture of the chordae tendineae, sudden left ventricular dilation (from myocarditis or ischemia) and mechanical failure of a prosthetic mitral valve.
- Chronic causes: mitral valve prolapse, infective endocarditis, rheumatic fever, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and dilated cardiomyopathy.

The leak sends extra blood back to the left atrium, which dilates with pressure and volume overload. The left ventricle then dilates with eccentric hypertrophy, which is systolic heart failure. Chronic disease goes on to pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure and finally combined right and left failure.

Mild-to-moderate isolated disease is usually silent, though palpitations can occur. Acute disease causes left-sided failure with dyspnea, orthopnea, rales and leg edema.

cards.t: Mitral regurgitation: the murmur and why squatting and handgrip make it louder
q: what is the murmur of mitral regurgitation
why does handgrip make mitral regurgitation louder
how is severe mitral regurgitation defined
cards.x:
The mitral regurgitation murmur is holosystolic (it fills the whole of systole) and blowing, heard at the apex, best with the patient lying on the left side. It spreads to the axilla, and there may be a third heart sound or a thrill.

Maneuvers that raise resistance against the ventricle's ejection make it louder, because more of the blood is pushed back through the leaky valve into the left atrium. That is why squatting and handgrip increase it, while standing and Valsalva decrease it.

Diagnosis: the transthoracic echocardiogram shows the regurgitant flow, left atrial enlargement and left ventricular hypertrophy. The electrocardiogram can show left atrial enlargement, with left ventricular hypertrophy in severe disease (low sensitivity). Left heart catheterization is not required. Severe mitral regurgitation means a regurgitant fraction of 50% or more, so half the blood leaks backward.

cards.t: Mitral regurgitation: medical treatment and when surgery is done
q: how is mitral regurgitation treated
when does mitral regurgitation need surgery
what is a mitral valve clip
cards.x:
Medical treatment has two aims: increase forward cardiac output while reducing the regurgitant volume (the amount of blood leaking backward), and treat the conditions that come with it, such as atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.

Surgery is for severe disease that causes symptoms. It is also done without symptoms once the left ventricle shows strain: an ejection fraction of 60% or less, or a left ventricular end-systolic dimension of 40 mm or more. The options are:
- a mitral valve clip, a catheter-based repair
- transcatheter mitral valve replacement, a stented valve delivered by catheter
- a mechanical valve, which needs lifelong anticoagulation
- a biological valve, which needs none

cards.t: Mitral valve prolapse
q: what is mitral valve prolapse
what is the classic finding in mitral valve prolapse
does mitral valve prolapse need treatment
cards.x:
Mitral valve prolapse is when the mitral valve leaflets flare back into the left atrium during systole. The cause is myxomatous degeneration of the valve. It usually affects healthy women aged 15 to 30.

It is usually benign and has no symptoms. The classic finding is a mid-systolic click at the apex. The echocardiogram shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets (over 5 mm).

Treatment is usually none. The thing to know is that some patients go on to develop mitral regurgitation, with its own symptoms and signs. If that happens, it is treated as mitral regurgitation: a clip, transcatheter mitral valve replacement, or a biological or mechanical valve replacement.

cards.t: Pulmonic stenosis
q: what is pulmonic stenosis
what does the pulmonic stenosis murmur sound like
how is pulmonic stenosis treated
cards.x:
Pulmonic stenosis is obstruction of the right ventricle's outflow of blood to the lungs. It is almost always congenital, commonly as part of tetralogy of Fallot, and carcinoid disease is another cause.

The right ventricle has to push against the block, so pressure rises and the muscle thickens (right ventricular hypertrophy, a diastolic failure pattern). With volume overload it dilates into right heart failure, a systolic pattern.

Mild to moderate disease is usually silent. Severe disease causes exertional dyspnea, fatigue, angina and syncope, and later right heart failure with an enlarged liver, ascites and edema.

The murmur is harsh, high-pitched, crescendo-decrescendo and mid-systolic, at the left second to fourth intercostal space. It gets louder with inspiration and comes with a split second heart sound. The electrocardiogram shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Mild to moderate disease needs no treatment and has a 94% 20-year survival. Severe disease with symptoms is treated with diuretics and pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty, and severe congenital disease may need valve replacement. Refer to cardiology if it is seen on echocardiogram.

cards.t: Pulmonic regurgitation and the Graham Steell murmur
q: what is the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation
what is the Graham Steell murmur
how do maneuvers change the pulmonic regurgitation murmur
cards.x:
Pulmonic regurgitation is incomplete closing of the pulmonic valve, so blood flows back into the right ventricle. The most common cause of significant regurgitation is iatrogenic: it is caused by medical treatment, for example a surgical valvotomy, valvectomy or valvuloplasty done to relieve right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Overall, though, the mild regurgitation seen with pulmonary hypertension is more common. Other causes are a congenital bicuspid valve and carcinoid disease.

Blood flowing back overloads the right ventricle, leading to right-sided heart failure with fatigue, peripheral edema, jugular venous distension and ascites.

The murmur is brief, decrescendo and early diastolic at the second left intercostal space. When the regurgitation comes from pulmonary hypertension it is high-pitched and called the Graham Steell murmur. It is soft and hard to hear. More venous return makes it louder (inspiration, squatting, lying supine); less makes it softer (expiration, standing).

It is usually an incidental finding on echocardiogram or exam. Treatment is of the underlying condition, with referral when it is seen on echocardiogram or there are right heart failure signs.

cards.t: Tricuspid stenosis
q: what causes tricuspid stenosis
what does the tricuspid stenosis murmur sound like
how is tricuspid stenosis treated
cards.x:
Tricuspid stenosis is obstruction of blood flowing from the right atrium into the right ventricle across a narrowed tricuspid valve. The most common cause is rheumatic fever, usually alongside rheumatic mitral disease. Carcinoid disease is the other notable cause. Congenital tricuspid stenosis is rare. It is most common in women.

The right atrium dilates and thickens, cardiac output is low, and the liver and portal system become congested. The result is right-sided heart failure without right ventricular dysfunction.

Mild to moderate disease is usually silent. Severe disease causes a fluttering discomfort in the neck, cold skin (from low output) and right upper quadrant pain (an enlarged liver). The murmur is a soft opening snap followed by a mid-diastolic rumble at the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid, louder with inspiration, with distended neck veins. The electrocardiogram shows right atrial enlargement out of proportion to right ventricular hypertrophy.

Severe symptomatic disease gets a low-salt diet, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist. A bioprosthetic valve replacement is preferred; balloon valvotomy or repair is reserved for liver congestion that may lead to cirrhosis or severe systemic venous congestion.

cards.t: Tricuspid regurgitation
q: what causes tricuspid regurgitation
what does the tricuspid regurgitation murmur sound like
how is tricuspid regurgitation treated
cards.x:
Tricuspid regurgitation is incomplete closing of the tricuspid valve, so blood flows from the right ventricle back into the right atrium. The most common cause is dilation of the tricuspid annulus (the ring the valve sits in), which follows right ventricular dilation in pulmonary hypertension. The primary cause to remember is infective endocarditis in people who inject drugs: when endocarditis is on the tricuspid valve, it is usually from intravenous drug use.

The murmur is holosystolic at the left mid or lower sternal border near the epigastrium, and it gets louder with inspiration. Other findings are raised jugular venous pressure with neck pulsations and a venous thrill over the right jugular vein. Mild to moderate disease is usually silent; severe disease causes pedal edema and ascites.

The echocardiogram with Doppler shows the leak and prolapsed, scarred or displaced leaflets. Treat the underlying condition. If the annulus is dilated, annuloplasty is used; if the cause is primary, the valve is repaired or replaced. Refer when it is seen on echocardiogram or with right heart failure symptoms.

cards.t: Carvallo sign: telling tricuspid from mitral regurgitation
q: what is the Carvallo sign
how do you tell tricuspid regurgitation from mitral regurgitation
why does the tricuspid regurgitation murmur get louder with inspiration
cards.x:
Carvallo sign is a right-sided murmur that gets louder with inspiration. It is the tool for separating tricuspid regurgitation from mitral regurgitation, two holosystolic murmurs that can sound alike.

The logic: breathing in increases venous return to the right side of the heart. A leak of the tricuspid valve sits on that side, so its murmur grows louder as more blood flows through. Mitral regurgitation is a left-sided murmur, so it does not grow louder on inspiration.

So if a holosystolic murmur gets louder when the patient takes a deep breath in, think tricuspid regurgitation.

cards.t: Mechanical vs biological replacement valves
q: when is a bioprosthetic valve preferred
what is the difference between a mechanical and a biological valve
do biological valves need anticoagulation
cards.x:
A mechanical valve needs anticoagulation for life. A biological (bioprosthetic) valve needs no anticoagulation beyond the immediate postoperative period.

Choosing between them: a biological valve is preferred when the patient's life expectancy is shorter than the valve's expected longevity, or when there is any contraindication to anticoagulation. By age, the standard is a mechanical valve for a younger patient and a bioprosthetic or transcatheter valve for an older one.

The contraindication is the key point: a patient who cannot safely take anticoagulants should not get a mechanical valve, because it would be left without the anticoagulation it requires.

cards.t: Mechanical valves: warfarin, INR targets and bridging with heparin
q: what INR target is used for a mechanical aortic or mitral valve
why is bridging needed for a mechanical valve
which anticoagulant is used for a mechanical valve
cards.x:
For mechanical valves, a vitamin K antagonist is recommended over no vitamin K antagonist and over antiplatelet agents, and the most commonly used one is warfarin. Warfarin is the only anticoagulant that works well with a mechanical valve.

The international normalized ratio (INR) target, which measures how thin the blood is, depends on where the valve is:
- Mechanical aortic valve: 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0).
- Mechanical mitral valve: 3.0 (range 2.5 to 3.5).
- Both aortic and mitral: 3.0 (range 2.5 to 3.5). With both valves, stick with the higher target.

If surgery requires stopping warfarin, a patient at higher clot risk is bridged with heparin until the INR is therapeutic again. The word to remember is bridge, and the bridging drug is heparin. Bridging with heparin is for a mechanical valve at higher clot risk (any mitral valve, an older-generation valve, or an aortic valve with atrial fibrillation, prior clot or a low ejection fraction); a bileaflet mechanical aortic valve with none of those risks usually does not need a bridge.

cards.t: Myocardial ischemia: an oxygen supply and demand mismatch
k: why does the heart get ischemic
q: what is myocardial ischemia
what causes ischemia of the heart muscle
how long until ischemic heart muscle is permanently damaged
cards.x:
Ischemia is a mismatch between what the heart muscle needs (oxygen demand) and what its blood supply delivers (oxygen supply). Think of it as the heart writing checks that its blood vessels cannot cash.
- Supply drops with atherosclerosis, a thrombus or embolus, anemia, spasm, dissection, carboxyhemoglobin (hemoglobin carrying carbon monoxide instead of oxygen) and hypoxia.
- Demand rises with exercise, emotional stress, left ventricular hypertrophy or cardiomyopathy, hyperthyroidism, hyperthermia and cocaine.

The heart is only 0.3% of body weight but uses 7% of the body's oxygen. Irreversible injury occurs in 40 to 60 minutes. Without enough oxygen the cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and lactic acid builds up. The damage comes from free radicals, lactic acid and calcium building up inside the cells.

This is why angina comes with exertion: exercise raises demand, a narrowed artery cannot raise supply to match, and the mismatch produces pain.

cards.t: Hypokinesia, akinesia and dyskinesia (wall motion abnormalities)
q: what is the difference between hypokinesia, akinesia and dyskinesia
what are regional wall motion abnormalities
cards.x:
Regional wall motion abnormalities are areas of the heart wall that move abnormally, and they are seen on an echocardiogram. There are three words to keep apart:
- Hypokinesia: reduced movement of that part of the wall.
- Akinesia: no movement at all.
- Dyskinesia: bulging wall movement, where the segment bulges out instead of squeezing in.

cards.t: The coronary arteries: what each feeds and which is the usual culprit
q: which coronary artery is most often blocked in a heart attack
what does the right coronary artery supply
why does a right coronary infarct cause heart block
cards.x:
There are three main coronary arteries: the right coronary artery, the left anterior descending (LAD) and the circumflex. The LAD has a new name, the anterior interventricular artery.

In an acute infarction, the most common culprit is the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) at 40 to 50%, then the right coronary artery at 30 to 40% and the left circumflex at 15 to 20%. ST elevation in leads V1 through V4, the anterior and septal leads, points to the anterior interventricular artery.

The right coronary artery supplies the atrioventricular node, so a right coronary infarct is more likely to cause dysrhythmias, and a patient who develops complete heart block during an inferior infarct most likely has a right coronary lesion. Heart block can also occur with a large anterior infarct, which carries a worse outlook. The sinoatrial node is supplied by the right coronary artery in 60% and the circumflex in 40%, so you cannot know for sure.

The left ventricle is supplied by the anterior interventricular, circumflex, left marginal and diagonal branches, and the interventricular septum is mostly supplied by the left coronary. Left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality.

cards.t: Papillary muscle blood supply and acute mitral regurgitation
q: why does a heart attack cause acute mitral regurgitation
which artery feeds the papillary muscles
what is the mitral apparatus
cards.x:
The papillary muscles are the small muscle columns inside the left ventricle. Through the chordae tendineae (the thin cords attached to the valve leaflets) they hold the mitral valve closed. Together the leaflets, chordae and papillary muscles are the mitral apparatus.

If a heart attack damages a papillary muscle and it ruptures, the valve can no longer close, which is a cause of acute mitral regurgitation. Rupture of the chordae tendineae can do the same.

Which artery matters depends on the muscle:
- The anterolateral papillary muscle is supplied by the anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex.
- The posteromedial papillary muscle is supplied by the posterior interventricular branch.

cards.t: Atherosclerosis and plaque rupture (why an acute coronary syndrome happens)
q: what is atherosclerosis
what happens when a plaque ruptures
what is the difference between a stable and an unstable plaque
cards.x:
Atherosclerosis is a build-up in the artery wall of fat, smooth muscle, fibroblasts and extracellular matrix. Macrophages become foam cells and sit under a fibrous cap.

The cap is what decides how dangerous the plaque is. A stable atheroma has a thick fibrous cap covering its necrotic core. A thin-cap fibroatheroma has only a thread-like cap between the core and the open channel of the artery (the lumen).

If the cap ruptures, platelets are activated and tissue factor sets off the clotting cascade, which lays down fibrin. The result is a thrombus on the cholesterol-rich core, which is the clot behind an acute coronary syndrome.

cards.t: Coronary artery disease risk factors (modifiable and nonmodifiable)
q: what are the risk factors for coronary artery disease
what family history counts as a risk factor
which risk factors can you change
cards.x:
Risk factors split into the ones you cannot change and the ones you can.

Nonmodifiable:
- Age: 45 or older in men, 55 or older in women.
- Sex: men carry more risk than premenopausal women, but the gap narrows with age.
- Family history: sudden death or infarction in a male first-degree relative before age 55, or a female first-degree relative before age 65.

Modifiable: obesity, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, smoking, hypertension, excessive alcohol, a sedentary lifestyle and ineffective stress management. Smoking is a strong predictor, especially in women under 45.

cards.t: Angina pectoris: what it is and what the pain is like
q: what is angina pectoris
what does typical cardiac chest pain feel like
what is Levine's sign
cards.x:
Angina pectoris is transient myocardial ischemia that is not long or severe enough to cause an infarction, and the symptoms recur. The pain is not affected by position and typically worsens with exertion, since the more the heart works, the higher its demand. Pain that changes with position lowers the suspicion that it is cardiac.

"Typical" cardiac chest pain is substernal chest pressure that is worse with exertion, radiates to the neck or shoulder, comes with shortness of breath and sweating (diaphoresis), and is relieved by nitroglycerin. Patients describe it as squeezing, tightness, pressure, constriction, burning, heartburn, fullness or band-like, and sometimes as a toothache.

Levine's sign is a clenched fist held over the sternum while describing the discomfort. It is the classic gesture of ischemic chest pain.

cards.t: Silent ischemia: ischemia without chest pain
q: why might a diabetic patient have a heart attack without chest pain
what are the atypical symptoms of ischemia
cards.x:
Chest discomfort may be absent even when the heart is ischemic. This is seen with diabetes mellitus, peripheral neuropathy, a transplanted heart, problems with the nerves that carry pain (afferent dysfunction) and differences in pain threshold.

Instead the ischemia presents as shortness of breath, cough, nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain, sweating, dizziness or lightheadedness, or fatigue. That is why each of these questions matters in the history.

cards.t: Where chest pain from different organs is felt
q: where is referred pain from a heart attack felt
where is the pain of aortic dissection
how does the location of pain help tell the cause
cards.x:
Pain from different organs tends to land in different places, which helps point to the cause:
- Acute coronary syndrome: most commonly the jaw, teeth or arm. It can also be felt in the back, the scapular region or the epigastric or left upper quadrant area.
- Thoracic aortic dissection: the left side or between the shoulder blades (interscapular).
- Pancreas: straight through to the back.
- Gallbladder: the right scapular region.
- Aneurysm: the back.

cards.t: The initial workup for chest pain
q: what tests does every chest pain patient get
which labs are ordered for chest pain
what is the first test for chest pain
cards.x:
Every chest pain patient gets a chest radiograph and an immediate (stat) electrocardiogram, which is the first test of the workup.

Labs that are definitely sent: complete blood count, metabolic panel, prothrombin and partial thromboplastin time, troponin, and lipids (which can wait until later). Tests that are maybe sent, depending on the picture: a drug screen, D-dimer, lipase and pro-B-type natriuretic peptide.

cards.t: Chest pain risk scores: HEART and TIMI
q: what is the HEART score
what TIMI score means early invasive treatment
what do risk scores for chest pain tell you
cards.x:
Risk scores predict the chance of a bad outcome, and there are several of them. Two are worth knowing.

The HEART (History, electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors, initial Troponin) score is built from exactly those five pieces. The risk factors counted are diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, smoking and a family history of coronary disease, and known coronary disease counts more. If the troponin is elevated, the score matters much less, because an elevated troponin overrides everything else.

The Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) score is used for unstable angina and non-ST-elevation infarction. A score of 3 or higher justifies an early invasive approach, because that patient will need intensive care or emergency revascularization. It is the interventionalist's score.

cards.t: Coronary calcium score, stress tests and other cardiac tests
q: what is a coronary calcium score used for
is a calcium score used to diagnose acute coronary syndrome
what test follows an abnormal nuclear stress test
cards.x:
A cardiac computed tomography calcium score (0 to 400 or more, with higher meaning more risk) is used for risk stratification, estimating future risk. It is not used to diagnose or treat acute coronary syndrome.

Other diagnostic tests for suspected coronary disease:
- Stress testing: a treadmill electrocardiogram or a nuclear stress test. If the nuclear stress test is abnormal, the next step is cardiac catheterization.
- Echocardiogram.
- Coronary computed tomography angiography.

cards.t: Troponin: what it is, the cutoffs and what it can tell you
q: what is the cutoff for an abnormal troponin
what is high-sensitivity troponin
does a normal troponin rule out a heart attack
cards.x:
Troponins are protein molecules found in cardiac and skeletal muscle, but not in smooth muscle. There are three types: I, T and C, and troponin I is specific to the heart.

The numbers to know:
- Standard troponin I: above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal (0.04 or less is not abnormal; 0.05 or higher is abnormal).
- High-sensitivity troponin I: 12 ng/L in women and 20 ng/L in men.

Say "not abnormal", not "negative". Troponin is better at ruling people out than ruling them in. It tells you who can safely go home; it does not tell you who is definitely having a heart attack. The high-sensitivity assay is why a woman whose value the old test called normal is no longer sent home.

Troponin is also what separates unstable angina (normal) from non-ST-elevation infarction (elevated).

cards.t: Serial troponins: why one troponin means two
q: why do you repeat a troponin
what does a rising troponin mean
can a patient go home with a low troponin
cards.x:
When you draw one troponin, you draw a second, because the change over time is what matters. If the second value is above the cutoff (for example the women's 12 ng/L for high-sensitivity troponin I) and also higher than the first, the troponin is rising and abnormal: more heart cells are dying, so another is ordered. A rising troponin I together with an ischemic picture (symptoms or electrocardiogram changes) means an infarction. A rise alone means injury to the heart muscle, which has other causes too.

The same logic can send a patient home. Two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L, far below the men's cutoff of 20 ng/L, together with a normal electrocardiogram, rule out an infarct.

cards.t: Stable angina (stable ischemic heart disease)
q: what is stable angina
how is stable angina diagnosed
how is stable angina different from unstable angina
cards.x:
Stable angina is the most common form of angina pectoris. It is usually brought on by activity and relieved by rest and nitroglycerin. That relief is what separates it from unstable angina, where pain comes at rest.

Diagnosis: a stress test (exercise treadmill or nuclear stress) shows ischemia: ST depression on the electrocardiogram, or a reversible defect on the nuclear images. Coronary angiography, where a catheter is placed and dye is sprayed to image the arteries, is the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease.

Treatment: sublingual nitroglycerin, lifestyle modification, a beta blocker (a calcium channel blocker if beta blockers are contraindicated), a statin and aspirin. Aspirin prevents future attacks in chronic stable angina and in survivors of an acute coronary syndrome. Clopidogrel is the alternative if aspirin cannot be taken. Aspirin plus clopidogrel together is used after an acute coronary syndrome or a stent, not routinely for chronic stable angina.

cards.t: Nitroglycerin for angina and what to tell the patient
q: how does nitroglycerin relieve angina
when should a patient with angina call emergency services
does nitroglycerin treat the disease
cards.x:
Sublingual nitroglycerin is the cornerstone of angina therapy. It is primarily a venodilator: widening the veins lowers preload, which lowers wall stress and oxygen demand, and it dilates arteries too. It treats the pain, not the disease.

Patient education: if the pain is not better, or is worse, 5 minutes after the first dose, call 911 (emergency medical services). Further doses can be taken every 5 minutes, up to three, while waiting for help.

cards.t: Stable angina vs unstable angina vs NSTEMI vs STEMI
k: how to tell unstable angina from NSTEMI
q: what is the difference between unstable angina and NSTEMI
what are the acute coronary syndromes
how do the electrocardiogram and troponin differ across angina and infarction
cards.x:
The acute coronary syndromes are unstable angina, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Here is how they differ on the electrocardiogram and troponin:
- Stable angina: changes appear only on a stress test, usually ST depression.
- Unstable angina: non-specific changes, usually inverted T waves, with pain at rest. Troponin is normal.
- NSTEMI: ST depression over 1 mm and/or T-wave inversion in two or more consecutive leads. Troponin is elevated.
- STEMI: ST elevation over 1 mm in two or more consecutive leads. Troponin is elevated.

The key line is that troponin differentiates unstable angina (normal) from NSTEMI (elevated).

cards.t: Reading a stress test: ischemia vs infarction
q: what does a reversible defect on a nuclear stress test mean
what does a non-reversible defect mean
cards.x:
On a nuclear stress test, a reversible perfusion defect means ischemia: the area gets too little blood under stress but recovers at rest. A non-reversible (fixed) defect means infarction, where the muscle is already dead.

A stress test can show ST depression, or just T-wave inversion, when the heart is stressed.

cards.t: Unstable angina: what changes from stable angina
q: what makes angina unstable
is unstable angina an emergency
cards.x:
Unstable angina is a change in a patient's stable angina. Any of these makes it unstable: the pain occurs at rest, it is new in onset and limits activity, or it is increasing, with more discomfort and more often. Nitroglycerin usually, but not always, helps.

It is an acute coronary syndrome and a medical emergency. The troponin stays normal, which is what separates it from a non-ST-elevation infarction.

cards.t: Treatment of unstable angina and NSTEMI (and the oxygen rule in MONA)
q: how are unstable angina and NSTEMI treated
what is MONA
when do you give oxygen in a heart attack
cards.x:
A non-ST-elevation infarction is treated the same as unstable angina, as a medical emergency:
- Chewable aspirin.
- A beta blocker to reduce oxygen demand, and intravenous nitrates if appropriate.
- Antithrombotic therapy: typically dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel), with or without an anticoagulant.

The old memory aid MONA (morphine, oxygen, nitroglycerin, aspirin) is an older approach. Give oxygen only if oxygen saturation is below 91%. Over-oxygenating these people can make things worse, and with normal oxygen levels it causes peripheral vasoconstriction.

After initial stabilization: left heart catheterization, coronary angiography, and angioplasty or percutaneous coronary intervention. Then exercise as tolerated, a low-salt, low-fat diet, hydration and scheduled follow-up.

cards.t: Which leads point to which wall and artery
q: which leads show an inferior infarction
which artery matches which leads on the ECG
how do I remember the lead groups
cards.x:
The leads that show ST changes name the wall involved, and the wall names the likely artery:
- II, III and aVF: inferior wall, right coronary artery (and/or circumflex).
- I, aVL and V5 to V6: lateral wall, circumflex (or a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending).
- V1 to V4: anterior and septal wall (V1 and V2 septal, V3 and V4 anterior), left anterior descending.
- V1 and V4R (a right-sided lead): the right ventricle, right coronary artery.

Memory aids: "Inferior = right coronary artery". For the limb leads, "my patients are ill": more I's than L's, so II, III and aVF are inferior and I and aVL are lateral. For V1 to V6, "A-S-S up, A-L-L down": V3, V2, V1 are anterior, septal, septal, and V4, V5, V6 are anterior, lateral, lateral.

cards.t: Subendocardial vs transmural ischemia, and how an ST-elevation infarct evolves
q: why does subendocardial ischemia cause ST depression
what are the electrocardiogram stages of an ST-elevation infarction
what do Q waves mean
cards.x:
Subendocardial ischemia (the inner layer of the wall) causes ST depression over that region. Transmural ischemia (through the full thickness of the wall) causes ST elevation.

An ST-elevation infarction changes over time on the electrocardiogram:
- Minutes to hours: hyperacute T waves and ST elevation.
- Hours to 1 day: ST elevation with T-wave inversion and a Q wave.
- About 1 week: a Q wave with a "coronary T".
- Months: a persistent Q wave.

Pathologic Q waves mean the infarction has already happened.

cards.t: Posterior myocardial infarction (ST depression in V1 to V3)
q: how do you recognize a posterior infarction
what are posterior leads
why is posterior MI easy to miss
cards.x:
A posterior infarction is easy to miss. It shows as ST depression in V1 to V3, because that is the mirror image (reciprocal) of ST elevation on the back wall of the heart. Flip the tracing upside down and it looks like an ST-elevation infarction.

The fix is to get posterior leads (V7 to 9, which makes a 15-lead electrocardiogram) to confirm it. The culprit is the right coronary or the circumflex artery.

cards.t: STEMI: what defines an ST-elevation myocardial infarction
k: new left bundle branch block STEMI equivalent
q: what is a STEMI
does a new left bundle branch block count as a STEMI
what are reciprocal changes
cards.x:
An ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), also called a transmural infarction, is myocardial necrosis with ST elevation (over 1 mm) in two or more consecutive leads that is not quickly reversed by nitroglycerin. There is reciprocal ST depression on the opposite side of the heart, and Q waves.

Current guidelines no longer treat a new or presumed-new left bundle branch block alone as a STEMI equivalent, because the block hides the ST segment. With ongoing ischemic pain, hypotension or heart failure it is managed like a STEMI, with the catheterization team. Otherwise it is judged on the rest of the picture.

cards.t: STEMI treatment: time is muscle
q: what is the treatment for a STEMI
what is the door-to-balloon goal
which drugs are given in a STEMI
cards.x:
In an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), time is muscle: the faster the blocked artery is opened, the more heart muscle is saved. The electrocardiogram is done within 10 minutes of arrival, and the goal door-to-balloon time is under 90 minutes.
- Give chewable aspirin and call the cardiac catheterization (percutaneous coronary intervention) team.
- Once catheterization is confirmed, add a second antiplatelet drug that blocks a platelet receptor (P2Y12 receptor antagonist: ticagrelor, prasugrel or clopidogrel) and a heparin drip.
- Nitroglycerin (sublingual every 5 minutes, paste or infusion) and a beta blocker if there is no bradycardia. Nitroglycerin is not given in a right ventricular infarct.

Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors have fallen out of favor. If the closest percutaneous intervention unit is 2 or more hours away, give thrombolytics (clot-busting drugs) instead, started within 30 minutes of arrival.

cards.t: Thrombolytics in STEMI: when, which drugs and who cannot have them
q: when are thrombolytics given in a STEMI
what is the most common thrombolytic
what are the contraindications to thrombolytics
cards.x:
Thrombolytics (clot-busting drugs) are given when the closest percutaneous intervention unit is 2 or more hours away, and they are started within 30 minutes of arrival. Tenecteplase is the most common today. Others are alteplase, reteplase, streptokinase, anistreplase and lanoteplase. The main risk is intracerebral hemorrhage.

Contraindications fall into two groups. The first group is the list below down to uncontrolled hypertension; the second, labeled potential serious bleeding, starts at severe diabetic retinopathy:
- active bleeding or a known bleeding disorder
