- major surgery or trauma in the last 4 weeks
- any previous intracranial (brain) hemorrhage, or an ischemic stroke within the last 3 months
- pregnancy
- uncontrolled hypertension (over 190/100 mmHg)
- severe diabetic retinopathy, current oral anticoagulation, a recent non-compressible vascular puncture, or prolonged (over 5 minutes) or traumatic cardiopulmonary resuscitation

cards.t: Nitroglycerin and oxygen cautions during a heart attack
q: when is nitroglycerin contraindicated
why ask women about phosphodiesterase inhibitors
when should you give oxygen in a heart attack
cards.x:
Two medication cautions come up in infarction care.
- Oxygen is given only if oxygen saturation is below 91%. With normal oxygen levels, do not give it, because it causes peripheral vasoconstriction.
- Nitroglycerin must not be given to a patient who has recently taken a phosphodiesterase inhibitor for erectile dysfunction. Ask women too, because the same drugs treat pulmonary arterial hypertension.

A separate nitroglycerin rule applies to a right ventricular infarct, covered in its own card.

cards.t: Right ventricular infarct: why nitroglycerin is dangerous
q: why can't you give nitroglycerin in a right ventricular infarct
how do you recognize a right ventricular infarct
does every inferior infarct mean no nitroglycerin
cards.x:
A right coronary occlusion affects the inferior and posterior wall of the left ventricle and the septum, and in 15 to 30% it extends into the right ventricle. The sign is ST elevation in V1 and V4R (a right-sided lead).

Do not give nitroglycerin. The injured right ventricle depends on preload to keep pumping (the Frank-Starling effect: more filling leads to a stronger squeeze). Nitroglycerin drops preload, so the push is lost, output falls further, and the patient goes into shock or right-sided heart failure.

The rule applies to a right ventricular infarct, not to every inferior infarct.

cards.t: Why nitroglycerin is avoided when the heart depends on preload
q: when should nitroglycerin not be given
why are nitrates avoided in aortic stenosis
what do aortic stenosis and a right ventricular infarct have in common
cards.x:
Nitroglycerin is mainly a venodilator: widening the veins lowers preload (the filling of the heart), which lowers wall stress and oxygen demand. That is why it helps angina. It is a problem when the heart cannot do without that filling.
- Aortic stenosis: these patients are preload dependent, so nitrates are avoided if angina is present, along with dehydration and strenuous exertion.
- Right ventricular infarct: the injured right ventricle depends on filling (the Frank-Starling effect: more filling leads to a stronger squeeze). Nitroglycerin drops preload, so output falls further and the patient goes into shock or right-sided heart failure. The rule is for a right ventricular infarct, not for every inferior infarct.

A third caution has a different reason: recent use of a phosphodiesterase inhibitor for erectile dysfunction.

cards.t: Catheterization, angiography, angioplasty and PCI: what each word means
q: what is the difference between angiography and PCI
what is percutaneous coronary intervention
what is atherectomy
cards.x:
Four terms get mixed up, so here is what each one means:
- Left heart catheterization: a guidewire is introduced to reach the chambers of the heart and/or the coronary arteries. It is the tube that goes in.
- Coronary angiography: dye is used to identify the lesion. It is the gold standard for diagnosing coronary disease.
- Coronary angioplasty: a device "balloons" open a narrowed artery. Plain old balloon angioplasty opens the artery without a stent.
- Percutaneous coronary intervention: the umbrella term for any catheter-based treatment of a coronary artery, including balloon angioplasty, atherectomy and placing a drug-eluting or non-drug-eluting stent. If anything is done while in there, it is a percutaneous coronary intervention.

During an intervention the options are balloon angioplasty (dilates the vessel), atherectomy (physically removing atheroma, calcium and excess cellular material) and stent placement, usually after balloon pre-dilation.

cards.t: After a stent: why dual antiplatelet therapy cannot be stopped early
q: why must patients keep taking clopidogrel after a stent
what happens if you stop dual antiplatelet therapy early
what medicines follow a stent
cards.x:
After a stent, medical optimization means dual antiplatelet therapy (P2Y12 receptor antagonist such as clopidogrel, plus a cyclooxygenase inhibitor, aspirin), a statin and an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, with anticoagulation if indicated.

Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy in the first 6 weeks is the strongest predictor of stent thrombosis, a sudden clot in the stent that can cause a large, often fatal infarction. The event is thrombosis, not restenosis (re-narrowing). The patient has to take the medicines.

In a patient who will not take them, think of bypass surgery or balloon angioplasty rather than a stent.

cards.t: Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)
q: what is a coronary artery bypass graft
which vessel is used first for bypass
where is the graft attached
cards.x:
A coronary artery bypass graft reroutes blood around a blockage. The surgeon connects (anastomoses) one or both mammary arteries or a radial artery to the coronary artery beyond (distal to) the obstruction. Arteries are used first.

A vein is also commonly used, especially for additional vessels or when an artery cannot be used. It is usually the great saphenous vein, and it connects the aorta to the coronary artery beyond the obstruction.

cards.t: Complications after a myocardial infarction (including Dressler syndrome)
q: what are the complications of a myocardial infarction
what is Dressler syndrome
which infarcts cause cardiogenic shock
cards.x:
Complications of an infarction include post-infarction ischemia, congestive heart failure, myocardial rupture, ventricular aneurysm, thromboembolism, pericarditis (Dressler syndrome), cardiogenic shock and arrhythmias.

Cardiogenic shock is more common in left-sided infarcts, and left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality.

Dressler syndrome is pericarditis after an infarct. Pleuritic chest pain with a pericardial friction rub weeks after the infarct points to the pericardium rather than the ventricle.

cards.t: Medications and prevention after a myocardial infarction
q: do beta blockers help after a heart attack
do calcium channel blockers improve survival after a heart attack
which drugs are used to prevent another heart attack
cards.x:
After an infarct, control the risk factors: blood pressure, lipids and glucose, plus weight loss, alcohol restriction, exercise, smoking cessation and stress management.
- Beta blockers improve survival when the ejection fraction is reduced; the benefit is not established with a preserved ejection fraction.
- Calcium channel blockers do not improve prognosis. Diltiazem and verapamil have no mortality benefit after infarction; they relieve angina or control rate when a beta blocker cannot be used, and they are avoided with a reduced ejection fraction or heart failure.
- A high-intensity statin (atorvastatin or rosuvastatin) goes to every acute coronary syndrome patient, regardless of baseline LDL (low-density lipoprotein) cholesterol, started before discharge.
- ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors reduce remodeling (scarring) and are indicated with reduced left ventricular function, to prevent dilation and heart failure.
- Aspirin is recommended, and clopidogrel is necessary after a stent. Warfarin is not routine; it is added only when an anterior infarct leaves an akinetic apex (may be considered) or a left ventricular thrombus.

cards.t: Sudden cardiac death
k: sudden death first sign of coronary disease
q: what is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death
how often is sudden death the first sign of coronary disease
cards.x:
The most common cause of sudden cardiac death is ventricular fibrillation. In over 20% of people with coronary disease (about one in five) it is the first sign the disease was there.

Other causes are left ventricular hypertrophy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypoxia and electrolyte abnormalities.

cards.t: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina: what it is and when it strikes
q: what is Prinzmetal angina
what causes vasospastic angina
when does vasospastic angina occur
cards.x:
Vasospastic angina, also called Prinzmetal, variant or coronary vasospasm angina, is caused by spasm of a coronary artery in normal or diseased arteries. The arteries are not blocked up, but they spasm shut. It is relatively uncommon, often under age 50. It occurs at rest and responds to nitroglycerin.

Cigarette smoking is a major risk factor. Drugs may precipitate it: cocaine, ephedrine, marijuana, alcohol, amphetamine and triptans.

The pattern is a chronic one of recurrent rest pain, most often between midnight and 8 in the morning. It comes and goes gradually and lasts 5 to 15 minutes (episodes may last longer). The pain is "typical" chest pain.

cards.t: Vasospastic angina: diagnosis and what to avoid
q: how is vasospastic angina diagnosed
what is the first-line treatment for vasospastic angina
which drugs should be avoided in vasospastic angina
cards.x:
During an episode, the electrocardiogram shows transient ST elevation: ischemic ST changes in multiple leads that resolve, without a cause for increased oxygen demand. Angiography shows no high-grade coronary stenoses.

The gold standard is to provoke the spasm during angiography with ergonovine or acetylcholine, then relieve it with nitroglycerin given through the catheter. The diagnosis is made when the provoked spasm is seen and then goes away with a squirt of nitroglycerin.

Treatment: stop smoking, use nitrates for symptoms, and use calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, amlodipine) first line. Avoid nonselective beta blockers and triptans. High-dose aspirin may worsen spasm; low-dose aspirin is usually continued if there is also atherosclerotic coronary disease.

cards.t: Microvascular angina (formerly cardiac syndrome X)
q: what is microvascular angina
who gets microvascular angina
how is microvascular angina diagnosed and treated
cards.x:
Microvascular angina, formerly called cardiac syndrome X, is angina with ST changes but normal coronary arteries on the angiogram. It is more frequent in females and often associated with stress or anxiety.

It is a diagnosis of exclusion, and angiography is required to rule out coronary artery disease. Proposed mechanisms include endothelial dysfunction, insulin resistance or diabetes, abnormal autonomic control, estrogen deficiency and altered pain perception.

Treatment is very similar to coronary disease: lifestyle and risk-factor reduction, a calcium channel blocker, a beta blocker, an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor and a statin.

Do not confuse it with MINOCA (myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries). MINOCA is an infarction, with a troponin rise, while microvascular angina has no infarction.

cards.t: Heart failure: definition, how the body compensates and what remodeling does
k: how does the body compensate for heart failure
q: what is heart failure
what are the four mechanisms of heart failure
how does the body compensate in heart failure
cards.x:
Heart failure is the inability of the heart to pump blood at a rate that meets the body's metabolic demands at rest and during effort, or doing so only with abnormally high filling pressures. It is a complex clinical syndrome (a group of signs and symptoms) that can result from any structural or functional disorder that impairs the ventricle's ability to fill with or eject blood, with effort intolerance, fluid retention and reduced longevity.

Four basic mechanisms produce failure: excessive preload (too much blood volume), excessive afterload (too much resistance), decreased contractility and decreased filling.

The body answers increased demand three ways: a faster heart rate, stronger contraction and more preload. These help at first and later drive damage. Acute damage or chronic conditions drive cardiac remodeling: myocyte hypertrophy and collagen fibrosis. In that picture, the sympathetic and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone systems worsen the damage, while the natriuretic peptides are the beneficial compensation.

cards.t: Causes of heart failure: ischemic vs non-ischemic cardiomyopathy
q: what causes heart failure
what is the difference between ischemic and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy
what is the most common valvular cause of heart failure
cards.x:
Most heart failure comes from a problem of the heart muscle or the load on it, and the causes are sorted into two groups: ischemic and non-ischemic.

Ischemic cardiomyopathy comes from an infarction (myocardial infarction), ongoing ischemia (persistent or chronic intermittent) or shock (hypoperfusion).

Non-ischemic cardiomyopathy is everything else: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypertension, valvular disease, dilated cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, toxins (alcohol, chemotherapy), and autoimmune or metabolic disease (diabetes, thyroid disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus).

For valve disease, the most common valvular cause is aortic stenosis. Mitral stenosis appears instead as a cause of right-sided failure.

cards.t: Heart failure: how common it is and its risk factors
q: how common is heart failure
what are the risk factors for heart failure
which heart failure risk factors can be changed
cards.x:
Heart failure is common. 6.7 million Americans older than 20 have it (2025). About 60% of patients are older than 65, and in that group one-year mortality after a hospitalization is 35%. Among people older than 80, 10 to 15% have it, and the lifetime risk is 24% (1 in 4). It accounts for 45% of cardiovascular deaths.

Risk factors: age, hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes, chronic tachyarrhythmias, obesity or metabolic syndrome, excessive alcohol, tobacco, family history, genetic abnormality and cardiotoxic medications.

Counseling targets the modifiable ones. Tobacco, excess alcohol and obesity can be changed; age, family history and genetic abnormality cannot.

cards.t: Systolic vs diastolic heart failure: the two chains
k: S3 vs S4 in heart failure
q: what is the difference between systolic and diastolic heart failure
why does diastolic failure have a normal ejection fraction
which heart sound goes with systolic and diastolic failure
cards.x:
Systole is the squeeze, so systolic heart failure is a problem of contraction. Diastole is the rest, so diastolic heart failure is a problem of relaxation. Each one is a chain, so spot one clue in a question and you can fill in the rest.

Systolic chain: thin, dilated (ballooned) muscle that contracts poorly and has lost elasticity, as in ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy. Ejection fraction is reduced, blood pressure is normal or low, the heart sound is a third heart sound (S3, from rapid filling of the dilated ventricle), and the congestion is pulmonary.

Diastolic chain: thick, enlarged muscle that contracts strongly but relaxes poorly, as in a heart thickened by long-standing hypertension (hypertensive heart disease) or in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Ejection fraction is preserved, the heart sound is a fourth heart sound (S4, from strong atrial contraction against the thick left ventricle), and blood pressure is high. The congestion is pulmonary, as in systolic failure, and leg swelling can also occur.

Add an elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) to either chain and you have the diagnosis.

cards.t: Ejection fraction and the heart failure categories
q: what ejection fraction counts as reduced, mildly reduced and preserved
what is improved ejection fraction
what is a normal cardiac output
cards.x:
Ejection fraction is the percentage of the filled (end-diastolic) volume that the ventricle ejects with each beat. Cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate. A normal cardiac output is 5 to 6 liters per minute, and a normal ejection fraction is 50% or more. The big dividing line in treatment is 40%: at 40% or less the full set of drugs is recommended, while 41 to 49% and 50% or more are managed similarly.

The four categories:
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF): 40% or less.
- Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFmrEF): 41 to 49%. These cutoffs are exact.
- Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF): 50% or more.
- Heart failure with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF): it was 40% or less and is now over 40%.

History decides the label. An ejection fraction that climbs from 30% to 46% is improved, not mildly reduced, even though 46% on its own would sit in the 41 to 49% band. Someone who has recovered is treated differently from someone who was never reduced.

cards.t: NYHA functional classes I to IV
q: what are the NYHA classes
what is NYHA class III
how do NYHA classes differ from heart failure stages
cards.x:
The New York Heart Association (NYHA) class grades symptoms, so it describes how the patient feels now:
- Class I: no symptoms.
- Class II: symptoms with exertion.
- Class III: symptoms with slight exertion.
- Class IV: symptoms at rest.

The class describes symptoms right now. That is different from the stages of the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association, which describe the natural history of the disease and never move backward.

cards.t: Heart failure stages A to D
q: what are the stages of heart failure
what is stage B heart failure
does a patient move back a stage when symptoms resolve
cards.x:
The stages, from the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association, describe natural history and do not move backward.
- Stage A, at risk: risk factors, normal heart function, no symptoms.
- Stage B, pre-heart failure: asymptomatic structural heart disease (ischemic cardiomyopathy, systolic dysfunction, diastolic dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy).
- Stage C, symptomatic: symptomatic structural heart disease, past or current. Once symptoms have occurred, resolution on treatment does not move the patient backward, so symptoms that have resolved still mean stage C.
- Stage D, advanced heart failure.

So a patient who felt better on treatment is still stage C. The New York Heart Association class, by contrast, describes current symptoms and can change.

cards.t: Heart failure drugs at stage A and stage B (SGLT2 inhibitor first)
k: first medication in at-risk heart failure
q: what is the first drug for an at-risk patient with diabetes
when does a beta blocker enter heart failure therapy
what drugs are used in stage B heart failure
cards.x:
For an at-risk patient with diabetes, the first recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin, not a beta blocker.

By stage:
- Stage A (at risk): an SGLT2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes (strong recommendation). No beta blocker yet.
- Stage B (pre-heart failure): an SGLT2 inhibitor in diabetes, an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan if the ACE inhibitor is not tolerated, and a beta blocker. All are strong recommendations.
- Stages C and D: therapy is chosen by ejection fraction group.

cards.t: Heart failure symptoms and signs: volume overload and poor perfusion
q: what are the symptoms of heart failure
what is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
what are the signs of poor perfusion in heart failure
cards.x:
Clinical heart failure means signs and symptoms of heart failure from a structural or functional cardiac abnormality, plus one of two things: an elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or objective evidence of cardiogenic pulmonary or systemic congestion.

The picture has three parts:
- Volume overload: dyspnea on exertion, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (waking up breathless), orthopnea (breathless lying flat), pulmonary or peripheral edema, elevated jugular venous pressure, tachycardia, and a third and fourth heart sound.
- Inadequate tissue perfusion: weakness, fatigue, lethargy, malaise, syncope, near-syncope and obtundation.
- Renal dysfunction: acute kidney injury and decreased urine output.

cards.t: Warm/cold, wet/dry: the bedside profiles of heart failure
q: what do warm and wet or cold and dry mean in heart failure
what are the signs of congestion in heart failure
what are the signs of low perfusion
cards.x:
At the bedside, heart failure is sorted by two questions: is the patient congested (wet or dry), and is the tissue perfused (warm or cold)?
- Warm and dry: normal.
- Warm and wet: congestion.
- Cold and dry: hypoperfusion.
- Cold and wet: both.

Signs of low perfusion: narrow pulse pressure, sleepy or obtunded, low serum sodium, cool extremities, hypotension with an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor and renal dysfunction.

Signs of congestion: orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, jugular venous distension, hepatomegaly, edema and rales (rare in chronic heart failure).

cards.t: Congestive heart failure is a clinical diagnosis (and needs congestion)
q: how is congestive heart failure diagnosed
does heart failure require edema
why isn't fatigue and shortness of breath enough for congestive heart failure
cards.x:
Congestive heart failure is a clinical diagnosis: signs and symptoms of heart failure plus an elevated B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or cardiogenic pulmonary or systemic congestion. No single test makes the diagnosis alone.

The word that matters is congestion. A clinical diagnosis requires congestion, and congestion means edema, pulmonary and/or peripheral. Fatigue and exertional dyspnea without any edema do not make it congestive.

cards.t: Which tests are used in heart failure and what each one tells you
k: chest x-ray heart failure Kerley B lines
q: what does the chest radiograph show in heart failure
which test is most accurate for ejection fraction
why check a metabolic panel in heart failure
cards.x:
Heart failure is worked up with several tests, and each has a job:
- Echocardiogram: most accurate for structures such as valves, classifies by ejection fraction, and is the definitive test for right-sided failure.
- Multigated acquisition (MUGA) scan: a very accurate and reproducible measure of ejection fraction (it does not assess perfusion). If it disagrees with the echocardiogram on the ejection fraction, trust the MUGA scan. If it disagrees with the echocardiogram on the ejection fraction, trust the MUGA scan.
- Chest radiograph: pleural effusion, cephalization of vessels, Kerley B lines and an increased cardiothoracic ratio.
- Complete blood count: the differential diagnosis, for example anemia.
- Complete metabolic panel: electrolytes, potassium above all, and renal function (blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, filtration rate).
- Troponin: only with concern for a non-ST-elevation infarction or heart failure secondary to ischemic cardiomyopathy.
- Electrocardiogram: ischemic changes, left ventricular hypertrophy (tall R in V5 to V6, deep S in V1 to V2) and right heart strain (right axis deviation, right bundle branch block, T-wave inversion in V1 to V3).

cards.t: BNP vs NT-proBNP: what each is and the cutoffs
q: what BNP rules out acute heart failure
what is the difference between BNP and NT-proBNP
what is the cutoff for BNP over 900
cards.x:
B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and the newer pro-B-type natriuretic peptide test (NT-proBNP) are blood tests that rise when the heart muscle is under strain, and their cutoffs differ, so know which one was done.

BNP is a bioactive hormone secreted mainly by the ventricular heart muscle in response to wall stress from volume or pressure overload. It rises over 1 to 3 hours and peaks at 12 hours. It is degraded by neprilysin, so sacubitril-valsartan alters it.
- Rule out acute heart failure: under 100 (negative predictive value above 90%).
- Gray zone: 100 to 400, with no useful sensitivity or specificity.
- Likely heart failure: over 400. Likely acute heart failure: over 900.

NT-proBNP measures an inactive precursor fragment. It is more stable, peaks at 24 hours, is detected earlier and stays detectable longer, and neprilysin does not degrade it.
- Rule out acute heart failure: under 300 (negative predictive value above 90%).
- Likely acute heart failure: above 450 if younger than 50, above 900 if 50 to 75, above 1800 if older than 75. In a stable outpatient, an NT-proBNP under 125 makes heart failure unlikely.

cards.t: Heart failure treatment: goals and the main drug classes
q: what are the goals of heart failure treatment
what drug classes are used in heart failure
who gets hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate
cards.x:
Treatment has three goals: decrease symptoms, increase survival and limit disease progression. That is why the regimen continues after the patient feels better: feeling better meets only the first goal.

The main classes:
- Potassium-wasting diuretics: thiazide-like (hydrochlorothiazide, metolazone) and loop (furosemide, bumetanide). Monitor potassium and renal function.
- ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, angiotensin receptor blocker or angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor: lisinopril and enalapril; losartan, valsartan and irbesartan; sacubitril-valsartan.
- Beta blocker.
- Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor: dapagliflozin, empagliflozin.
- Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist: spironolactone, eplerenone (a potassium-sparing diuretic).
- Nitrates: isosorbide dinitrate, together with hydralazine, for a selected group (African American patients in New York Heart Association class III to IV).

cards.t: Guideline-directed therapy: reduced vs preserved vs mildly reduced
q: how does heart failure treatment differ by ejection fraction
which drugs are strong recommendations in reduced ejection fraction
is treatment for HFpEF and HFmrEF similar
cards.x:
Guideline-directed medical therapy is the set of drugs recommended for heart failure, with each recommendation graded strong, moderate or weak. For preserved and mildly reduced ejection fraction it is very similar; for reduced ejection fraction it is different.
- Reduced ejection fraction: an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (New York Heart Association class II to III) or an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (class II to IV), a beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor and diuretics as needed are all strong. Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate is strong for African American patients with New York Heart Association class III to IV.
- Preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction: diuretics as needed are strong, and the SGLT2 inhibitor is moderate. Where they are listed, the other classes are weak.

In reduced ejection fraction, therapy is prioritized for the patient's comorbidities and optimized as the patient is hemodynamically stable: each class is raised as blood pressure and tolerance allow.

cards.t: Diuretics in heart failure: potassium-wasting vs potassium-sparing
q: which heart failure diuretics waste potassium
why check potassium and renal function in heart failure
is spironolactone potassium-sparing
cards.x:
Diuretics are used as needed for congestion. The potassium-wasting ones are the thiazide-like diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, metolazone) and the loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide). Because they waste potassium, potassium and renal function are followed on the complete metabolic panel.

Spironolactone and eplerenone, the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, work the opposite way. They are potassium-sparing diuretics, so potassium is checked with them too, along with renal function.

cards.t: Heart failure: calcium channel blockers to avoid, and inotropes
q: are calcium channel blockers safe in heart failure
when are inotropes used in heart failure
can I use diltiazem for rate control in heart failure
cards.x:
The calcium channel blockers to avoid in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction are the non-dihydropyridine type; amlodipine is neutral. Verapamil and diltiazem are both in that group, even when planning something like rate control in atrial fibrillation. Blood pressure is controlled by optimizing the recommended classes as tolerated, and a beta blocker belongs to core therapy.

Inotropic therapy (dobutamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, milrinone) is for intensive care use only.

cards.t: Defibrillators in heart failure: implantable vs wearable
q: when is an implantable defibrillator indicated
what is a wearable defibrillator vest for
what happens after acute heart failure from an infarction with a low ejection fraction
cards.x:
An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator protects against sudden death. It is indicated for ischemic or non-ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 35% or less, New York Heart Association class II to III, on optimal guideline-directed therapy, with a life expectancy of at least one year. The reason is that 52% of cardiac arrests in hospitalized patients with reduced ejection fraction are due to ventricular arrhythmias.

After acute heart failure (from infarction, sepsis and similar) with an ejection fraction under 35%, the pathway is different: a wearable defibrillator vest, then optimized therapy and cardiac rehabilitation, then a repeat echocardiogram. The implantable device follows only if there is no improvement; implanting one right away is premature.

cards.t: Sacubitril-valsartan and why it matters for BNP
q: what does sacubitril-valsartan do to BNP
which natriuretic peptide test is not affected by neprilysin
when is an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor used
cards.x:
Sacubitril-valsartan is the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, a heart failure drug that combines an angiotensin receptor blocker (valsartan) with a neprilysin inhibitor (sacubitril). Neprilysin is the enzyme that breaks down B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP).

That matters when you read the blood test. A BNP level is altered by sacubitril-valsartan, because neprilysin degrades BNP. The pro-B-type natriuretic peptide fragment (NT-proBNP) is not the one neprilysin degrades, so the drug does not alter it. So know which test was done and whether the patient takes this drug.

In reduced ejection fraction, the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is a strong recommendation for New York Heart Association class II to III, where an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker covers class II to IV.

cards.t: Left-sided heart failure
q: what is left-sided heart failure
how common is left-sided heart failure
what does left-sided failure cause on the right side
cards.x:
Left-sided heart failure is failure of the left ventricle, and it is the most common type by far, at 70 to 80% of all heart failure. The failing ventricle can be systolic or diastolic, ischemic or non-ischemic, and with a preserved or reduced ejection fraction.

Its mark is pulmonary congestion: orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and crackles. Systolic failure comes with normal or low blood pressure, a third heart sound (S3, rapid filling of a dilated left ventricle) and pulmonary edema. Diastolic failure comes with hypertension, a fourth heart sound (S4, atrial contraction against a hypertrophic left ventricle) and the same pulmonary congestion as systolic failure.

Chronic left-sided failure is the most common cause of right-sided failure.

cards.t: Right-sided heart failure
q: what causes right-sided heart failure
what are the signs of right-sided heart failure
why is right-sided failure worse than left-sided
cards.x:
Right-sided heart failure is failure of the right ventricle, so blood backs up into the body instead of the lungs. The most common cause is chronic left-sided heart failure, which progresses from left failure to right hypertrophic to right dilated cardiomyopathy. Mitral valve stenosis and pulmonary arterial hypertension are two more causes.

Systemic overload gives peripheral edema and jugular venous distension. Portal overload gives nausea, loss of appetite and hepatomegaly (congestion, ascites).

With mitral stenosis there is a rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap. With tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary arterial hypertension there is a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration.

Clinical heart failure with jugular venous distension raises suspicion, and the echocardiogram gives the definitive diagnosis. The electrocardiogram shows right heart strain. Management is symptom control, treating the underlying cause, heart transplant and palliative care. Right-sided failure generally carries a poor prognosis, and the outlook depends on the cause.

cards.t: Combined right and left heart failure
q: what is combined right and left heart failure
how is combined heart failure managed
cards.x: Combined right and left heart failure means both ventricles have failed. The usual route is chronic left-sided failure eventually reaching the right side. At this point management moves to symptom management, comfort care and transplant: when optimized therapy no longer controls the symptoms, transplant evaluation or comfort care is discussed.

cards.t: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (systolic)
q: what is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
how is reduced ejection fraction heart failure treated
what are the causes of systolic heart failure
cards.x:
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is the weak squeeze: failure of contraction (systolic function) with an ejection fraction of 40% or less. If it was 40% or less and is now over 40%, that is improved ejection fraction. The causes are ischemic cardiomyopathy (infarction, ischemia, shock) and dilated cardiomyopathy.

The clues are normal or low blood pressure, pulmonary edema and dyspnea, a third heart sound from rapid filling of a dilated left ventricle, and crackles. The echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 40% or less and the B-type natriuretic peptide is elevated.

Treatment: an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (New York Heart Association class II to III) or an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (II to IV), a beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor and diuretics as needed, all strong, plus hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate for African American patients with New York Heart Association class III to IV. A defibrillator is for ejection fraction of 35% or less, class II to III, on optimal therapy, with a life expectancy of at least one year.

cards.t: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (diastolic)
q: what is heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
what causes diastolic heart failure
how is preserved ejection fraction heart failure treated
cards.x:
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction is the stiff, thick ventricle that cannot relax: failure of diastolic function (relaxation) with an ejection fraction of 50% or more. The pattern to know is hypertension driving a thickened (hypertrophic) ventricle.

The clues are hypertension, a fourth heart sound from strong left atrial contraction against a hypertrophic left ventricle, and exertional breathlessness with lung congestion, often with leg swelling too. The echocardiogram shows a preserved ejection fraction and a left ventricular wall over 10 mm, which means hypertrophy. The B-type natriuretic peptide is elevated. The electrocardiogram shows a tall R in V5 to V6 and a deep S in V1 to V2.

Treatment: diuretics as needed (strong) and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor (moderate). An angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an angiotensin receptor blocker are weak. Other classes are used for comorbidities.

cards.t: Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction
q: what is heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction
how is mildly reduced ejection fraction treated
cards.x:
Heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction is an ejection fraction of 41 to 49% on echocardiogram that has never been 40% or less. Learn it as "mildly" reduced.

Treatment is very similar to preserved ejection fraction: diuretics as needed (strong), a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor (moderate), and an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, angiotensin receptor blocker, angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and beta blocker (all weak).

cards.t: Acute and acute decompensated heart failure
q: what is acute decompensated heart failure
how is acute heart failure treated
what BNP level rules out acute heart failure
cards.x:
Acute heart failure is sudden in onset: either new, or an exacerbation of existing disease. Chronic means more than 1 year, and an exacerbation once the disease has lasted over a year is "acute on chronic". The sequence runs from pre-heart failure (asymptomatic) to acute new-onset (symptomatic), resolution, exacerbation, chronic, then acute on chronic. Named precipitants include myocardial infarction and sepsis.

The picture is congestion (pulmonary and/or peripheral edema), dyspnea and crackles, sorted by the warm or cold, wet or dry profile. A B-type natriuretic peptide under 100 rules out acute heart failure and over 900 makes it likely, while the newer pro-B-type natriuretic peptide test (NT-proBNP) under 300 rules it out.

Treatment is diuretics for congestion, and inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone and others) in intensive care only. If the ejection fraction is under 35% after the event, a wearable defibrillator pathway follows. The outlook is serious: one-year mortality after hospitalization is 35% in those older than 65, each rise of 100 in B-type natriuretic peptide means a 35% higher relative risk of death, and a predischarge level under 430 means a lower risk of 30-day readmission.

cards.t: High-output heart failure
k: anemia hyperthyroidism arteriovenous fistula heart failure
q: what is high-output heart failure
what causes high-output heart failure
how is high-output heart failure treated
cards.x:
High-output heart failure is elevated cardiac output, from increased heart rate and contractility, driven by increased peripheral demand: the body is asking for more than the heart can comfortably give.

Causes include anemia, hyperthyroidism and an arteriovenous fistula. Symptoms are the heart failure syndrome: fatigue, dyspnea, edema and palpitations.

The workup is an echocardiogram, complete blood count, complete metabolic panel and B-type natriuretic peptide. The blood count matters because anemia is one of the causes. Treatment is to correct the underlying cause, with a diuretic for congestion. Over time, the increased demand may lead to ischemic cardiomyopathy or remodeling.

cards.t: Secondary hypertension: the one clue that names each cause
k: which clue points to which secondary cause
q: which clue points to which cause of secondary hypertension
what clue suggests primary aldosteronism
how do I tell the causes of secondary hypertension apart
cards.x:
Each major secondary cause of hypertension has one clue that points straight to it:
- Unexplained low potassium with resistant pressure: primary aldosteronism.
- An abdominal bruit, asymmetric kidneys or flash pulmonary edema: renovascular disease.
- A marked creatinine rise after starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor: bilateral renal artery stenosis.
- Loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness: obstructive sleep apnea.
- Proximal muscle weakness, bruising, thin skin and purple striae: Cushing syndrome.

Three more: attacks of pressure, perspiration, palpitations, pallor and tremor mean pheochromocytoma; radial-femoral delay with a leg pressure lower than the arm means coarctation of the aorta; and a raised systolic pressure with a fast heart rate points to an overactive thyroid, while a raised diastolic pressure with cold intolerance points to an underactive one.

cards.t: Blood pressure drug side effects: which class causes which
k: side effect names the drug class
q: which blood pressure drug causes dry cough
which drug class causes ankle edema and gingival enlargement
what are the side effects of clonidine and hydralazine
cards.x:
Many blood pressure drugs have a signature side effect, and the side effect usually names the class:
- Dry cough, high potassium and angioedema (swelling of the face, lips or throat): angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors.
- Dependent ankle edema, flushing and gingival enlargement: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.
- Bradycardia (a slow heart rate) and heart block, worse with a beta blocker: the non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, verapamil and diltiazem.
- Low sodium, low potassium, high uric acid and volume depletion: thiazide-type diuretics.
- Reflex tachycardia (a reflex speeding of the heart) and fluid retention: hydralazine.

One more: sedation, dry mouth and rebound hypertension when the drug is stopped abruptly point to a central alpha-2 agonist such as clonidine.

cards.t: Hypertension traps: what a normal result does not rule out
k: normal electrocardiogram does not exclude hypertrophy
normal office blood pressure masked hypertension
q: does a normal electrocardiogram rule out left ventricular hypertrophy
does a normal chest radiograph rule out aortic dissection
can heart failure occur with a normal ejection fraction
cards.x:
Four normal results sound reassuring and are not:
- A normal electrocardiogram does not exclude hypertrophy. The voltage criteria are specific but not sensitive, so they miss cases.
- A normal chest radiograph does not exclude aortic dissection, and neither do normal pulses.
- A normal ejection fraction does not exclude heart failure. Heart failure with a preserved ejection fraction is a recognized endpoint of hypertensive heart disease.
- Normal office readings do not mean normal pressure. Masked hypertension carries real cardiovascular risk.

cards.t: Hypertension traps: very high readings, resistance, drug pairs and fast lowering
k: is a very high blood pressure always an emergency
lowering blood pressure fast in an emergency
q: does a very high blood pressure reading always mean an emergency
does resistant hypertension always mean adding more drugs
is it safest to lower blood pressure quickly in an emergency
cards.x:
Four ideas that sound right and are wrong:
- A very high reading means an emergency. No numeric cutoff exists; acute organ injury is what defines it.
- Resistant pressure means more drugs are needed. Nonadherence is the most common cause, so check technique too.
- An angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor plus an angiotensin receptor blocker is a logical pair. It never is: it brings harm without benefit.
- Lowering the pressure fast in an emergency is safest. The organs have adapted (autoregulation), so rapid reduction causes ischemia.
